maintopic: REVISED REGULATIONS RESPECTING NORTHWEST TERRITORIES AND LAND UNDER TERRITORIAL WATERS

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: REVISED REGULATIONS RESPECTING NORTHWEST TERRITORIES AND LAND UNDER TERRITORIAL WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to announce the promulgation of revised mining regulations for the Northwest Territories, which are designed to ensure maximum benefit to Canadian interests and to make these regulations applicable to lands underlying territorial waters which are in federal jurisdiction.
The government's purpose in revising the Northwest Territories quartz mining regulations, which are now called the Canada mining regulations, is the same as in the case of the recently promulgated regulations applying to oil and gas. First, the revised regulations make provision for the disposition of mining exploration and development rights on federal land underlying territorial waters of Canada. Regulations covering lands not forming part of any province or territory have not existed in the past, presumably because the exploitation of offshore deposits has not been considered technically or economically feasible. Further, a convention adopted in Geneva in 1958 gave Canada the right to exploit the resources of its continental shelf. There are at the present time Canadian companies who want the right to explore on these lands. In this respect the present regulations do for minerals what the Canada oil and gas regulations do for the fossil fuels.
The second purpose of the revised regulations is to embody another step which the 79951-0-345
government is taking to ensure Canadians a full opportunity to participate in resource development. In the case of the oil and gas regulations the Canadian participation clauses become operative at the time an explorer for oil and gas converts a permit into a lease. This was the best time to apply this principle in the case of oil and gas, because in the permit stage a permit holder's rights are limited to the exploration and delineation of oil and gas resources. In order to exploit them he must have a lease.
However, in the case of minerals, the pattern of activity under the regulations which have been in force practically without change since 1932 allows not only exploration but also exploitation to be carried on before a lease is taken out. Under the regulations no one can acquire claims either by staking or assignment without holding a miner's licence. In order to be effective, therefore, the new Canadian participation clauses as applied to the present regulations must be applied from the outset as a requirement for obtaining a miner's licence. However, licences held by persons and corporations which cannot meet the Canadian participation requirement will remain valid until March 31, 1961.
I think I should make it clear that this requirement for Canadian participation at the exploration stage in mining is intended to be of interim application only. Officers of my department have for a considerable time been working on a general revision of the mining regulations with the objective of bringing them into line with modern prospecting and development techniques. During the next few months I will be holding conferences with representatives of the mining industry. Before the end of the present fiscal year I expect to formulate a completely new set of regulations suitable for modern times.
It is my intention to provide in the new regulations for a system similar to that now obtaining under the recently revised oil and gas regulations. This will make a clear distinction between the exploration and exploitation phases of mineral development, and will protect the right of Canadians to have an opportunity to participate at the ownership stage. Any person or corporation will be able to acquire a mining licence and to stake and develop mining claims. However, it will be necessary to take out a mining lease before a mine can be brought into

Inquiries of the Ministry production, and it is at this stage that the Canadian participation clauses will apply.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: REVISED REGULATIONS RESPECTING NORTHWEST TERRITORIES AND LAND UNDER TERRITORIAL WATERS

Mr. Speaker, the house will have listened with interest to the minister's statement to the effect that new mining regulations have been promulgated. In due course, during the minister's estimates, we shall have an opportunity of questioning him on these regulations. Meanwhile, perhaps I may be permitted to say it is to be hoped that they are somewhat clearer than the oil and gas regulations were when they were first issued. I believe the minister himself indicated that they caused some confusion in his mind. I think he said that a good lawyer could drive a coach and four through them.
The minister has mentioned that these regulations will apply to land under offshore waters. This is a very important aspect of the regulations, especially as they extend the offshore waters out to the limit of the continental shelf. This is a matter that is of very great interest to the provinces, and I can only express the hope at this time that the provinces have been consulted in regard to this aspect of the regulations and accept this extension of the right of the federal government to the land under those waters.

maintopic: REVISED REGULATIONS RESPECTING NORTHWEST TERRITORIES AND LAND UNDER TERRITORIAL WATERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have listened with a great deal of interest to the statement of the minister which in our view deals with a matter of the utmost importance to all of Canada, the development of resources on the continental shelf. On the basis of the statement of the minister it is most difficult to go into details at the moment, but we do want to say, so important is the matter and so great our interest in it, that we hope to go into it in more detail and have a full discussion when the minister's estimates are before us, after having had an opportunity to study the statement the minister has made.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-35, respecting the international boundary commission.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a short bill respecting the international boundary commission. It was introduced in the other place and there was given very careful consideration in a committee which proved to be unanimous. I do not intend to go back beyond the international boundary treaty of 1908, but those hon. members who are interested in the story of the various treaties under which the boundary between Canada and the United States was established will find the speech made in the other place by Senator Blois extremely informative and interesting.
The international boundary treaty of 1908 established the international boundary commission which is composed of two sections, a Canadian section and a United States section. By a further treaty in 1925, described as being to "define and complete the international boundary between Canada and the United States", the commissioners appointed under the 1908 treaty are responsible for continuous maintenance of the international boundary line, the boundary monuments and a cleared sky line vista along the line. The vista which of course is easily noticed when it runs through wooded areas is a strip 20 feet wide made up of 10 feet on the Canadian side of the boundary line and 10 feet on the United States side. Probably most hon. members will have seen portions of this boundary line in one part of Canada or another.
As hon. members are aware, treaties to which the United States is signatory are submitted to the United States Senate, and when
International Boundary Commission passed they become self-implementing; that is to say, they become the law of the land. In Canada the situation is different. Here, specific legislation is required if necessary in order to implement the treaty. This is the reason the present bill has been introduced. It will ensure that Canada is fully able to implement the 1925 treaty.
Hon. members may ask why it is necessary now, 35 years after Canada signed the international treaty, for it to receive implementing legislation. The fact is that during this period the Canadian international boundary commissioner has been able to carry out the 1925 treaty obligations because permission was asked before entering private land in the immediate boundary area, and because Canadian land owners were prepared to co-operate with him in carrying out his functions.
I should like to say at this point that the Canadian international boundary commissioner is an official of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The annual expenses which represent Canada's share of the maintenance of the international boundary are included in the annual estimates of that department.
The increasing development and use of land near the international boundary from coast to coast has led with increasing frequency to proposed encroachments upon the boundary area by buildings and other structures. For example, the Great Northern railway proposed in 1954 that they would build a station right on the boundary line between White Rock, British Columbia, and Blaine, Washington, with half of the station on the Canadian side and half on the United States side. This proposal was objected to by the departments concerned at that time and nothing was done about it. Last autumn, however, there was a renewal of the suggestion that this station should be built straddling the boundary line.
The legislation now before the house seeks in no way to expropriate or remove buildings and structures now existing within 10 feet of the boundary line. There are some buildings already up which do stand on this 10 feet. On the contrary, this legislation seeks only to prevent enlargements of existing buildings and structures, and to avoid having new buildings and structures erected in the future.
We believe that this legislation is desirable in order that Canada may fulfill her treaty obligations, and also to provide adequate protection for the system of monuments. The commissioner is responsible for repairing and replacing monuments. For example, if the bank of a river were to fall in and carry a

International Boundary Commission monument with it, replacement would be the responsibility of the commissioner. The legislation is also necessary in order to give the boundary commissioner legal access to the boundary area; to prevent unauthorized encroachments in this boundary area, and to facilitate the application of customs regulations. I am sure the Minister of Finance will be pleased to know that the bill involves no additional financial obligations.
That is a brief summary of the bill. We believe that under present day conditions it is essential that the Canadian member of the international boundary commission be given the powers which are set out in the bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING INTERPRETATION, POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a short, straightforward and, I think, non-contentious bill, and we on this side intend to support it. The bill itself and the remarks just made by the minister remind us that it deals with the boundary between Canada and the United States, the boundary to which it is essential to refer in every after-dinner speech as an undefended boundary; undefended, of course, in the sense that there are no fortifications on the border, but certainly not undefended when you try to get across it if you are evading customs, immigration or security regulations.
It reminds us, Mr. Speaker, that in the bad old days relations between the two countries were such that there was fear and hostility on the boundary and which in those days twice resulted in war. We Canadians with, of course, help from the mother country were more successful in defending our boundary in war than we have been successful since in defending it in peacetime against arrangements, agreements and arbitrations made by the mother country which at that time had responsibility for our foreign policy. In some cases the result of those arbitrations-and I do not know whether we could have done any better ourselves if we had been independent-so far as the boundary is concerned is obvious, if you take one glance at the map. It is obvious in British Columbia; it is obvious in New Brunswick and Quebec.
The boundary has been established by three major treaties; the treaty of Paris, which I think was made in 1784 and which brought to an end the war with the colonies; the treaty of 1818, which extended the boundary of that day to the Lake of the Woods, and the treaty of 1846 which I think completed the process of boundary delineation in a major sense to the Pacific ocean. But in addition to these three major treaties there have been a good many other treaty arrangements, as the minister pointed out. They were dealt with in a very interesting way in a debate


on this matter in the other house. It was shown in that debate, as indeed it is clear from our reading of history, that in subsequent arrangements and arbitrations, especially the arbitration referred to the emperor of Germany in connection with Pacific boundary matters, I think in the early part of this century that Canada did not come out very well. The Alaska boundary award of 1903 is one example in our history of an unfortunate boundary dispute with the United States; because, as hon. members I am sure will recall, that arbitration and the award from it which established the present boundary between Alaska and British Columbia was very much at the expense of Canada. As the records also make clear, if that award had not been accepted by the negotiators on the Canadian and British side, the president of the United States in those days, the redoubtable Theodore Roosevelt, was going to establish his own boundary. Perhaps if that contingency had arisen he would have been a little more reasonable, but it does remind us that we have not always been too successful in our boundary negotiations with the United States.
Perhaps the Panhandle may one day be, if not returned to Canada, but surely one of those days we shall be able to get access to the Pacific coast through it. As I understand it there is now no complaint between the two countries in respect of major boundary matters. For many years now there have been only minor differences, and they have all been settled peacefully. Indeed no question arises in our country as it might indeed have arisen in other countries in other parts of the world, of a terra uredenta.
This bill will facilitate the work of the international boundary commission and that, of course, is all to the good. Sometimes we forget-indeed we should remember-that while there have been complications as there has been work required in marking the land boundary between the two countries, a great deal of our boundary is through the middle of streams or lakes. That has its own difficulty and has brought about its own complications in our relations with the United States. There is no better illustration of that than in the negotiations leading up to the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. Hon. members know that in some parts of the country the boundary goes down the middle of a stream. That has had a very important effect on how the St. Lawrence seaway had to be built.
A good many Canadians-indeed, I have heard the statement made in this house, and I heard it made on television the other night by a professor of history and a great authority on United States-Canadian relations-have said that it would have been much better

if Canada had built the seaway alone, and that it was too bad we were not able to do so. The reason that could not be done without the approval of the United States lies in the nature of the boundary at that spot because the boundary runs right down the middle of the St. Lawrence. Because of that boundary line it would have been quite impossible to have built a purely Canadian seaway which included a power dam, because you could not very well have built a power dam half way across. The location of the boundary, quite apart from the effect of the treaty of 1908, made it impossible to build a seaway by ourselves alone, if the United States objected to it, as a national seaway by Canada, even without power development, if that work had any effect on the boundary water levels. Therefore, because of the nature of our boundary, it would have been impossible to build a St. Lawrence seaway alone if it had any serious effect on the boundary waters or if we wished to have a power development at the same time.
The minister has indicated that the boundary commission has been working since 1925, and indeed since 1908, without the necessity for this kind of legislation, and I think working very effectively. Perhaps I may pay my tribute to the work done on both sides by the commission. The United States side and the Canadian side have worked quite effectively together and have not for that purpose required legislation. But the nature of developments on the boundary, as the commission has pointed out, certainly makes it desirable now to facilitate that work, to make it easier and indeed in some cases I think perhaps to make it possible by establishing a legislative basis for it, by even at this late date, implementing the treaty of 1925. We on this side are very glad to support the bill for these reasons.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. G. Dinsdale (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING INTERPRETATION, POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to me to see this legislation come before the house today for the purpose of putting in statutory form provisions respecting the work carried on in connection with the international boundary between Canada and the United States since the year 1908. It seems to me it is rather unusual that we should have delayed until the present time the enacting of formal provisions respecting the activities of the international boundary commission, but I heartily endorse the procedure that is being followed in presenting this legislation this morning.
This is an occasion when we could indulge in speeches such as we often hear regarding the unique position of the Canada-United

States international boundary. Because of the nature of the relationships that have existed between the two countries down through the years there have been many interesting expressions with respect to those relationships and developments along the international boundary. I am delighted to see that arrangements are made in the bill to preserve the monuments and sites already established along the border.
In my own constituency a unique development took place in the 1920's which was spontaneously supported1 by people on both sides of the border, and has resulted today in a rather outstanding example of international co-operation. During the 1920's members of the national gardeners' association of the United States prompted by Dr. Henry Moore of Islington, Ontario, began to discuss the possibility of making use of the international boundary to emphasize the desire for peace that was felt so strongly following world war I. A decision was made to establish on the international border an international peace garden dedicated to the ideals felt so strongly at that time. In 1932, on the Manitoba-North Dakota boundary, the official opening took place of what has become known today as the international peace garden.
Very substantial areas of land in the Turtle mountain region were set aside in perpetuity by the Canadian government, the United States government and the state and provincial governments concerned, and the area has been marked by a monument suitably inscribed with these words:
We two nations dedicate this garden and pledge ourselves that as long as men shall live we will not take up arms against one another.
This is the kind of development, springing spontaneously from the hearts of the people themselves, which indicates that the work of the international boundary commission had sooner or later to become embodied in formal legislative form. Since 1932 there have been developments of many kinds on this significant site, which is strategically located. From the geographical standpoint it stands halfway between the Atlantic and the Pacific. It is also almost directly on the geographic centre of the North American continent.
Since 1932, in addition to the original cairn erected to commemorate the desire and striving for peace, a formalized botanical garden has been developed. A park area has been established with a very interesting arboretum. At the present time there is activity on foot to establish a peace chapel which will be erected on the highest point of the Turtle mountain area. It is reassuring to note that all these developments will be protected and preserved in the future by the passage of this legislation.

The government of Canada has expressed its interest in this development by financial support, as has the United States government, but I want to underline the fact that this support is incidental to the development of the gardens; because the chief support, both financial and in personal interest, has arisen largely from the voluntary efforts of organizations on both sides of the border. In recent years the daughters of the empire, service clubs on both sides of the border, women's institutes, the homemakers of America and others have all taken an interest in this development. During the past three years considerable cultural activity has emerged on the site of the international peace gardens, and it promises in the immediate future to develop into another school for fine arts located on the border. We have an international music camp, for example, that meets there every summer. Various international organizations are tending to concentrate their activities there, such as conventions and so on. We have a very fine international student discussion group which conducts a student seminar each fall on some aspect of international problems.
This is a subject on which 'I could spend some time this morning but I thought, Mr. Speaker, that the occasion of the introduction of this legislation in respect to the international boundary commission provided an opportunity to bring to the attention of the members of this house, as well as the people of Canada, the sort of work that has been going on spontaneously and voluntarily for two years and is now being recognized in this formalized way.

Its purpose was to alleviate the burden of the 17 per cent freight rate increase that had been authorized in November, 1958. The act made provision for the board of transport commissioners to require reductions, during a period not exceeding one year, in the class and commodity rates, other than competitive rates, that were in effect and taking the 17 per cent increase when the act came into force on July 8, 1959. It also made provision
Freight Rates Reduction Act for payments to the companies not to exceed in the aggregate $20 million, as reimbursement for the resulting reductions in their revenues.
The committee will be interested to know what reductions in freight rates were accomplished under the legislation. The board required the companies to reduce, effective August 1, 1959, the 17 per cent freight rate increase by seven percentage points, that is to make it 10 per cent instead of 17 per cent on the rates affected. As figures of traffic actually carried during the year became known, the board determined that it could make a further reduction of two percentage points, bringing the 17 per cent down to 8 per cent, and this reduction was made effective on May 6 on traffic carried thereafter.
The freight rate reductions will expire on July 31 next, unless provision is made to continue them; and as the royal commission is still engaged in its inquiry respecting the railway situation the government has concluded that the benefits of the Freight Rates Reduction Act should be continued for a further period not exceeding nine months from July 31 next. The proposed amendments are for that purpose.
As the committee knows, last year's bill was considered very fully by parliament and was examined thoroughly by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines of this house and also by the standing committee on transport and communications of the Senate. The proposed amendments will, as I said, extend the benefits of the act for a further period beyond July 31 next.
Mr. Chairman, at the conclusion of the debate on second reading of this bill I propose to move that the bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for examination. Certain members of the committee have intimated to me that they would like this to be done, and I have concurred in their request.

As the minister has stated, this provides for a reduction in freight rates over a period of nine months. The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Freight Rates Reduction Act to extend for not more than nine months the period during which the revised rates under the said) act shall be applicable and to increase the authorized expenditure under the act by an additional fifteen million dollars.

Freight Rates Reduction Act
The two questions which come to my mind on reading this resolution are, first of all, why there should be this period of nine months and, next, why the sum of $15 million. I presume the $15 million is the proportionate part of the $20 million which would be required for the full 12 months.
Then there is another question which arises. This other question is that by virtue of the statement made by both the Prime Minister and Minister of Transport, freight rates have now become frozen in this country. I think the present position of the application for a general increase in freight rates made by the railway association of Canada is as follows, and if I am incorrect I take it the minister will correct me. The order of the board of transport commissioners was, I believe, dated January 13, 1959 setting a date for the hearing for final relief requested in the application of the association, which application was dated September 16, 1958. The date of the hearing was set by order for May 19, 1959, and April 10, 1959 was the date set for filing the supplement to the application specifying the amount of increase sought by way of final relief.
On April 8, 1959 the railway association, in compliance with the above order of the board, filed a supplement to their application seeking authority for a general increase of 12 per cent in the level of freight rates and 20 cents per ton on coal and coke. The railway association on April 10 applied for postponement of the hearing of the supplementary application and the board postponed the hearing sine die.
The question which arises is this. Does the statement made by both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport with reference to the freezing of freight rates apply to the application which was made for an additional general increase of 12 per cent? I think it would be important for us to know what the position is in that respect. If it does, does it apply during the period of nine months only?

The order of the board No. 98424 which came into effect on July 10, 1959 referred to the statute, chapter 27, 7-8 Elizabeth II, an act to make provision for the reduction of certain class and commodity rates on freight traffic. It made operative the terms of the statute. By virtue of this order it then became possible for the railways to file amended tariffs with respect to which the act came into effect.
The question that comes to my mind now is this. Will this bill, when it is passed, become effective in the same way as did the bill last year under chapter 27, 7-8 Elizabeth II? Will the board of transport commissioners be required to pass a similar order to put this into effect?
Of course the main questions that come to mind are these. How has the act operated during the 12 months? What has been the effect of it? The minister has given one effect, where the reduction has been down to 8 per cent, which is all to the good and, I am sure, helpful all across Canada. I believe we should be given additional information as to how the act has operated in general. What has been the effect of these reductions on class and commodity rates? As the committee knows, there is no reduction whatever in so far as competitive rates are concerned. What has been the effect on the uniformity of the reductions? Why the nine months in the resolution, and why the $15 million? Again I say we are in full support of this legislation. We think it is good legislation, and that it will substantially assist those who are moving goods across Canada.

This resolution is made necessary because the royal commission has not yet reported on its inquiry into the freight rate structure and the question of equalization. Although the resolution will lead to the expenditure of another $15 million it will not mean any gain for the public by way of lower freight rates. It will merely mean that the present freight rate structure will be maintained for a nine-month period, presumably in the expectation that the royal commission will have reported by that time. Because this will prevent any increase in freight rates at this time we are pleased to support the motion.
This government has a varying record with respect to freight rates. It came into office on the definite commitment that under this administration freight rates would not be increased but would be equalized. I say that because of the repeated statements made by the Prime Minister and because of the action of the government before the 1958 election in disallowing a general 3.6 per cent increase in freight rates.
This resolution will continue the reduction by approximately 50 per cent in the last 17 per cent horizontal increase in freight rates. Even under the policy of this administration there has been an increase in freight rates. I have examined the result of general increases in freight rates since the end of the war, and have calculated that there has been a general increase of some 157 per cent.

A royal commission has been set up to inquire into the freight rate structure of this country. After this royal commission completes its work I believe the government should consider an inquiry into the railway services that are being provided in this country. Only time will tell whether railway freight rates in this country will in fact be equalized or at least made more nearly equal than they are now. If we as a parliament do everything we can by way of legislation, by way of a royal commission, by way of subsequent prevention of freight rate increases, and at the same time allow railway services to deteriorate, we may find that we have railway rates equalized or frozen and are in fact losing the railway services so essential to the country.
This may or may not, Mr. Chairman, be the most appropriate place to make this statement, but I feel the time has now come when there should be an exhaustive inquiry into railway services in this country with the object of maintaining services essential for the growth and development of this nation. As I see it today, railway services are getting into a terrible mess. Services are being curtailed at an alarming rate.
While it is exceedingly necessary to take this kind of action, which we in the C.C.F. support, we feel that other action to maintain the services of the railways is now urgently required. When we speak of subsidies on freight rates generally, we in the west sometimes get the impression that a great many people in Canada feel that any subsidy paid to the railways is paid on behalf of the western Canadian farmers. We in the Conservative party from the west do not accept this premise at all. There is just as much reason for a subsidy to be paid on behalf of western farmers as for a subsidy to be paid on account of competitive rates in central Canada. We feel that any subsidy such as this one is of benefit to all Canadians, to the manufacturers in eastern Canada and in central Canada, to the people who are in business on both our coasts, to material and grain going east, and to the products of Canada's economy generally. We feel very strongly on this matter. We feel that any such subsidy should not be considered as a subsidy to the farmer of western Canada.

Unfortunately, as far as I can see this was the position of the hon. member for Laurier a year ago when we discussed this matter quite fully in committee. While he expressed some pious hopes that the Crowsnest pass rates would not be affected, he felt that the objective could be attained by a subsidy of some kind or another. We do not accept this at all. We do not accept the premise that a subsidy is paid on our behalf alone.
The other important thing about the reduction in the class and commodity rates is the beneficial effect it will have on our pulp and paper industry, on our feed grain going east and on a great amount of material coming out to western Canada. Certainly at a time when we are trying to do everything we can to meet the cost-price squeeze of the western farmer this is going to help along that line. It will also help to prevent the machinery companies from having any further excuse to raise their prices because of freight rates.

Perhaps one of the better examples of how freight rates affect us is the recent disappointing decision of the board of transport commissioners with regard to rapeseed. Finally I should like to make one or two remarks about the railways themselves. It seems to me that they do themselves no credit if the only way they can economize is by discontinuing services. They are going into the trucking industry, and before they go into it they are determined to give away any business they did have. I refer to the recent action of the Northern Alberta Railways, which discontinued services that were important to the people there and failed to supply an alternative service. railways tell us they are going into the trucking business and, as I say, they seem intent on giving away express and other business before they get into the trucking business.

Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting patiently for the opportunity to speak on freight rates in general and freight charges on rapeseed in particular. I do not have anything to add to what I have said already on the subject, but I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport the fact that the situation has deteriorated much more and is worse than it was a few months ago.
Within the last month the board of transport commissioners found it wise, for reasons best known to themselves, to not classify rapeseed as a grain. The best authorities on agriculture and the best scientists having to do with grain and cereal plants testified at the hearing that rapeseed is a grain. However, the situation being what it is, the rape-seed industry of the west is faced with a serious problem. This year more than ever the rapeseed grower will be faced with unfair freight charges of 80 cents per hundredweight while his counterparts, the producers of other grains, will have to pay only 22 cents or 23 cents per hundredweight.
This year we will see the rapeseed crop increased from half a million to a million or a million and a half acres because of the fact that the farmers could not harvest their crops last fall and had to wait until spring to harvest them before planting new crops. The farmers were very late in harvesting their crops, and the only thing they could plant at that time was rapeseed, because it only takes about 60 to 70 days for the crop to mature. As I stated before, all indications are that we will be faced with a million or a million and a half acres of rapeseed.
I should like to emphasize most emphatically that unless the government undertakes measures to alleviate the situation, this young industry may suffer a blow from which it will never recover. Since this is the second
Freight Rates Reduction Act time that the board of transport commissioners has refused to classify rapeseed as a grain, the only hope this young industry now has is that the Minister of Transport and the government will reverse the decision or will implement other measures whereby higher freight rates will not be charged on rapeseed than are charged on wheat, oats or barley. As the spokesman for a constituency in which half of all the rapeseed grown in Saskatchewan is produced. I should like to bring this point to the minister's attention again and appeal on behalf of the growers that action be taken to alleviate this serious situation.

Mr. Chairman, we are strongly in favour of the bill. I want to take this opportunity to speak in order to correct the record. As the result of remarks on this issue that I made previously this session I have been accused by several union representatives of advocating compulsory arbitration in labour matters, because of my suggestion that ultimately the stage is going to be reached when a new formula will have to be found in order to take the railway wage problem out of the present jackpot in which it seems to be. In many people's minds, I think certainly in the minds of the western farmers, the reason for the Freight Rate Assistance Act and the problems that brought it about, was the result of the wage negotiations, the wage increase given to railway employees. This attitude is an understandable one in an economy such as ours, where groups tend to recognize their own interests and be critical of others.
This situation is very apparent, Mr. Chairman, in the negotiations that are now under way between the railways and the unions, with no one having any clear-cut idea how to solve the problem of this particular type of collective bargaining. I think it is going to be a long time coming, but sooner or later we must find a formula that will enable railway workers to have their legitimate bargain struck and at the same time put both the railways and the users of the railways in some position of understanding and appreciating just how much leeway should be given to railway management in making concessions to the unions in the bargaining process. I believe this situation will be a long time in coming, but we certainly need some kind of formula or standard.
There have been arguments in the past, Mr. Chairman, that the wage set-up in the white goods industry should be the standard; that has been the suggestion put forward quite often by dominion representatives. Recently the argument has been put forward by the company that there should be a completely

Freight Rates Reduction Act new basis. Sooner or later, because oi the interest that the government and the very-large government railroad have in this matter, and the way freight rates touch upon so many political, regional and industrial considerations, we have to find a way out of this dilemma.
The royal commission on transportation, as I have said before, needs our sympathies. I do not know what kind of recommendations it is going to make. This measure is a stopgap to give them a bit more time, which I know they need from being at some of their hearings and from reading reports. I suggest to the minister that he and his officials should be very much concerned with adumbrating now in their own minds a policy for the railways even before the royal commission report is in their hands, because it strikes me that the royal commission is quite limited in the scope of the recommendations it can make. The royal commission, in itself, is an interim measure. What we need is a long range or long term solution to this whole question of the position of the railways and their relationship to the treasury.
It is said that transport expenditures are beginning to shift more and more markedly in volume to the air rather than the rail field. We seem to have quite a bit of tidying up to do in the railway transportation field. We have a very large government railway with a substantial debt, and interest is not paid on that debt except in years in which the railway has a surplus. However, it does not appear as though that particular railway is going to reach a surplus position for some time. It seems to me it is the government's responsibility to arrive at a transportation policy that will enable the railways to go ahead. I cannot see how the royal commission is going to be able to do much more than make recommendations in so far as the Crows-nest pass rates are concerned.
I do not know whether the minister has noticed that the counsel for Manitoba, Mr. Morrow, has been going about to farm union groups and other groups on the prairies foreshadowing the solution to be arrived at by the royal commission. This seems to be that the Crowsnest pass rates will remain as they are but that the railways will be given a much freer hand in so far as the abandonment of lines may be concerned. There is a suggestion also that the railways should be given more scope in abandoning passenger services and other losing services of that nature. This procedure may commend itself to many members, just as the bill does, as a short-run solution to the problem, but it seems to me we have to arrive at something more substantial. In so far as abandonment is concerned,

we have to consider the plight of the people who are living along the lines that are to be abandoned.
The other question that is fundamental to the railway problem, and again it is tied up with this Freight Rate Assistance Act because here is where much of the pressures generate, is automation and the capitalization for mechanical improvements on the railways. Then there is the whole question of unemployment created by the railways because of these modern methods. The problem needs a bit of a Solomon, and I do not know whether the minister is that Solomon or whether his officials can be. Certainly a very great responsibility rests upon the cabinet in connection with this matter. The royal commission and this particular measure we are about to pass are both, by their very nature, interim measures for the railways.
It is apparent from the hearings that have been held by the royal commission and the number of considerations being taken into account that this problem affects every part of the country in some way or another. I only hope the minister is not taking it easy, hoping for the royal commission report to enable the government to make its next moves in this field. It certainly seems to me this is one field in which we need the very best contributions we can get from management, from labour and from the agricultural industry in particular, which finds railway transportation still so fundamental in bringing its goods to market.

Mr. Chairman, during the debate so far we have had very good contributions and a number of questions have been asked. I shall answer them as best I can. The hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Assiniboia asked some questions about the operations of the royal commission. One question was, what is the commission doing at the present time? The answer is that there is an interval between public hearings. The commission is continuing its investigations, separate and apart from public hearings, and is considering the very voluminous submissions and opinions which have been received to date. Approximately 110 briefs have been received.
Another question was what further hearings, if any, are scheduled by the commission, and where will they be held? The answer is that the commission has held hearings covering 80 days at Fredericton, Charlottetown, Halifax, St. John's, Newfoundland, Winnipeg, Regina, Edmonton, Victoria, Vancouver, Port Arthur, Quebec city, Toronto and Ottawa. The commission will hold further hearings at Montreal commencing on July 7 and at Ottawa commencing on September 12. Hearings will be held thereafter as may be

necessary, but the Ottawa hearings are intended to be the final hearings.
The third question was, when does the royal commission expect to complete its work and make its report to the government? The answer is that the commission has not indicated to me how soon it expects to complete its work and make its report. I do know it is carrying on its investigations just as quickly as it can, and I hope there will be no cause for any undue delay in the completion of the investigation. It is my hope the work of the commission may be completed by the end of the year, and that I may receive a report very soon after that.
The hon. member for Laurier asked how the act has operated during the 12-month period which will end on July 31. Between August 1, 1959 and March 31, 1960, the first eight months of operation under the act, $11,349,362 was expended. If operations in the remaining four months were the same as the first eight months, that would require a further expenditure of $5,674,684 or a total of $17,024,044.
It became evident to the board of transport commissioners several months ago that the $20 million was not being used up at the rate that had been anticipated because of the fall off in freight traffic, and that a further reduction in the 17 per cent freight rate increase could be made for the last four months of the term. Hence this is how the money is expected to be spent during the last four months of operation. The overlap of July payments into August at the reduced rates, that is shipments made in July not reaching their destination until August, is expected to use up $900,000. The increase in reduction from 7 per cent to 9 per cent from May 1 to July 31 is expected to use up $1,277,400; and the addition of lake and rail traffic, that is the payments to steamship lines which all occur from April 1 to July 31, is expected to use up another $300,000, for a total of $2,477,400. This will leave a balance of approximately half a million dollars, it is expected, at the end of the 12-month period.

As far as I know, I think it is fair to say that the opposition of every political party in this chamber is that the Crowsnest rates should not be tampered with and that, no matter what the report may be, the producers who today receive the advantages of the Crowsnest rates shall not be adversely affected.
There may or may not be some alternative method decided upon to relieve any burden the royal commission may find flows from the Crowsnest rates. I am not suggesting in any way that the Crowsnest rates are a burden. I do not believe they are a burden. But this government is on record in the past as being not only fully in support of the Crowsnest rates but determined, as a matter of government policy, that these rates shall not be tampered with. Every time a railway company goes before the royal commission and attacks the Crowsnest rates there is a feeling of uneasiness on the prairies; and this bogey of interference with the Crowsnest rates is raised from time to time.
I think the minister would be doing a real service to Canadians in general and to the people of western Canada in particular if he were prepared at this time to reaffirm the policy and attitude of the government as far as the Crowsnest rates are concerned. I am not endeavouring in any way to imply that the government's position in this regard is weakening, or that the position of the government is not clear. But because of these persistent and consistent attacks in the press by railway companies and by others who have their own axes to grind with regard to


the Crowsnest rates I think it would be a service to parliament if the minister would reaffirm the government's position in connection with these rates.
There is a second question I should like to ask the minister, and that has to do with the recent decision of the board of transport commissioners with regard to rapeseed. I agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson in his reference to the way the railway companies have been allowed to reduce services with very little thought, in his opinion and also in mine, to the loss of revenue to the railway companies themselves and certainly without any consideration for the communities involved. We feel that the board of transport commissioners has been somewhat lax in allowing this wholesale reduction of railway services.
With regard to the freight rates affecting rapeseed, it has been contended, and I think rightly so, that rape should be considered a grain for the purpose of freight rates. This has not been agreed to by the board of transport commissioners. In other words the board has made an adverse decision on this point. As has already been stated, the government has it within its power to set aside, alter or change in any way any ruling of the board. I believe that power is contained in section 53 of the Railway Act. I would ask the minister whether the government is in fact considering the possibility of making any change in the ruling, either by setting it aside or by amending it. This government-and I give it full credit-has on at least one occasion found it desirable to set aside a ruling of the board of transport commissioners. That precedent is at hand. I hope it will be followed in connection with rapeseed so that producers of rapeseed may be on the same basis as producers of other grains in the province.
I have, then, two questions to ask the minister; first, whether he will reaffirm the government's position with regard to the Crowsnest rate, and second, whether or not the government has under consideration this decision of the board of transport commissioners concerning rapeseed, and when an announcement may be made as to whether the government is upholding this decision or taking action to set it aside.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to constitute a Department of Forestry which shall be presided over by a Minister of Forestry to be appointed under the Great Seal of Canada, to authorize the appointment of a deputy minister by the governor in council and the necessary officers, clerks and employees in the manner authorized by law, and to provide for the transfer of certain officers and

subtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR CREATION OF NEW DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is preliminary to the introduction of a bill to set up a department of government. Possibly 1 might begin by referring particularly to the report of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. I think this report deserves study on the part of all hon. members. It represents the results of a very intensive consideration of the problem of our forests, and is indicative of the favourable results which can be secured through the medium of committees which give to the consideration of the problems they have placed before them that care, acumen and attention which marked the investigation, hearing of evidence and recommendations of this committee.
I refer particularly to two of the recommendations in the third report to the house dated July 4, 1959. In paragraph 57 at page 1175 of the committee proceedings the following appears:
Your committee strongly recommends consideration of steps which would widen the scope of the forestry branch, increasing its status in such a way that a deputy minister would be in direct charge. The fact that such a status, comparable to that of a department does not exist now reflects a lack of appreciation of the importance of the forest industries to Canada, in the past, now, and in the future. Other departments of government are considered essential to serve industries or aspects of our national economy which are of much lesser economic consequence.
Then at page 1176 we find the following:
Your committee recommends that the entomological and plant pathology research relating to trees and forests, now under the Department of Agriculture, be transferred to and co-ordinated directly with the recommended and expanded forestry department.
Again, at page 1177 we find the following in paragraph 70:
Your committee feels that Canada cannot afford to ignore a potential so great for lumber and pulp sales as is offered in the Orient and, therefore, it recommends that these markets be approached on an open minded basis. Study should be made of our changing share of traditional markets in the United Kingdom and the United States of America. A marketing section should be created within the proposed department of forestry to aid the Department of Trade and Commerce in the merchandising of our wood products.
These were several of the recommendations which at least formed the basis for the introduction of this resolution, following the passage of which the bill in question will be introduced.
Department of Forestry
While all the recommendations cannot necessarily be accepted at this time, and while in no way suggesting that the Department of Trade and Commerce has not carried out fully its responsibilities in connection with the marketing of lumber and such products, I thought I should place these various recommendations before the committee so that the comprehensive consideration given by the committee to this matter would be within the knowledge of hon. members.
The present function of the federal government with respect to forestry consists of providing for good management of the forests under its direct control, the extending of financial assistance to enable the provinces to intensify their efforts in specified phases of forest management, and the conduct of research relating to forest management and the utilization of forest products. During past years and at the present time research activities relating to forestry have been divided between two departments. The forestry branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is responsible for all aspects of forest management research except forest entomology and forest pathology, which are the responsibility of the research branch of the Department of Agriculture.
I might digress for a moment to say that this afternoon, by reason of my position, I am introducing this resolution, but the discussion and consideration thereof will be placed mainly upon the shoulders of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources under whose department this matter has been administered in the past.
A major reason for the establishment of the proposed new department is to bring together the research activities now conducted by two departments and thus to provide for better integrated and more effective research programs. In the past three years several of the provinces and many organizations representing various branches of the wood using industries have made urgent representations to the effect that the support being given to forestry and forest products research by the dominion government has not been commensurate with the significance of the forest industries to the national economy. When I mention the last three years I also know as a fact that similar representations were made prior thereto. From these representations and from other sources of information available to it, the government has concluded that the time has come when the dominion interests in forestry should be brought together in the hands of one minister.
I think I might commence by placing before the committee in summary form a few pertinent facts regarding the importance of
548S

Department of Forestry the forest industry to Canada. More than 40 per cent of the land area of the 10 provinces consists of productive forest land. This area, by way of comparison, is almost four times as great as the area devoted to agriculture, which in capsule form reveals the extent of our forest resources. The pulp and paper industry is Canada's largest manufacturing industry; the lumber industry still stands high on the list. These industries are distributed throughout the country from coast to coast, and in addition to producing products of great value they are among the major sources of employment. External trade in wood, wood products and paper yields a balance in Canada's favour far larger than that contributed by any of the other major commodity groups recognized in national statistics form. Furthermore, a very large proportion of that favourable balance becomes available in United States funds.
In the past two or three years there have been studies of the demands for paper products and various other products in general which have been projected for a period of from 10 to 15 years and beyond. These projections and forecasts indicate radical increases within the period of time mentioned. Further expansion of Canada's forest industry is certainly possible. We have the raw material resources, and given a sufficiently good standard of forest management, the expansion can be maintained on a continuing basis. However, if the drain on the forest is to be radically increased and, at the same time, forest devastation is to be avoided, there are serious problems in forest management and forest protection which must be overcome. All of this emphasizes the increasing need for research the aim of which would be the improvement in management and utilization of forest products. Such programs must be accompanied by more economic research in order to help ensure that Canadian products can be placed on world markets at acceptable costs.
The conduct of forest and forest products research has been for many years a function of the dominion government, which now has unusually well developed research facilities in this field, by a wide margin the strongest of those facilities. The research function is not the exclusive prerogative of the federal government but is shared by some of the provinces, the university forestry schools and the industry itself. I hope the new department will be able not only to intensify the efficiency of federal forest research but also help to bring about co-ordination of research programs conducted by other agencies. I believe this objective is necessary if Canada

is to meet the challenge which expanding world markets for forest products will present in the coming years.
I might point out that in September, 1959, the food and agriculture organization brought out a report dealing with paper and paper products which stated in summary form that while world demand for paper and paper products in 1955 amounted to 56 million metric tons, in 1965 it will amount to 88 million metric tons and by 1975 to 134 million metric tons. At the present time Canada supplies about 16 per cent of the world market. If we are to maintain this percentage it will be necessary to supply 14 million metric tons by 1965 or a 50 per cent increase over the basic year 1955. By 1975 Canada will have to supply 21 million metric tons or a 123 per cent increase over the basic year. Even though there is some unused capacity at present in this country there would seem to be good prospects for the Canadian paper industry to more than double its present production in 15 years.
I am not going to go into details as to the net value of the products of the forest and forest industries. I simply point to the general position of these industries as outlined in my remarks earlier. I think it will be generally agreed that these are industries which have inherent in them the possibility of vast developments over their situation today.
We now come to the question of responsibility. In no way is the government, having at all times stood solidly behind the need of preserving the constitution in its entirety, desirous of interfering nor would it for a moment countenance any interference or invasion of the constitutional responsibility of the provinces in this connection or in any other. We believe it is the duty of the federal government to provide for the best practical management of forests under its direct control, but the greater part of Canada's forests are administered by the governments of the provinces in which they are located. Section 92, subsection 5 of the British North America Act provides that the legislature of each province may exclusively make laws respecting "the management and sale of the public lands belonging to the province and of the timber and wood thereon". As I said a moment ago, this in effect gives to each province the exclusive right to manage publicly owned forests within its boundaries as it sees fit, and I reiterate and make it explicitly clear that the new department will in no way infringe upon or impinge on any of the rights and jurisdiction of provincial governments.
On the other hand, those federal activities relating to forest and forest products research

and the financial assistance offered to the provinces to help to improve the management of their forests are carried on primarily for the benefit of the provinces themselves and to help the forest industries. More specifically, research findings of the dominion government are made available to provincial forest administrators and industrial forest operators so that they may make such use thereof as they deem fit and proper.
The proposal to establish a department of forestry reflects the realization of the importance of the forest industries and the resource on which they depend for raw materials. It will provide for more effective use of the resources available for promoting better forest protection and management and better use of the wood that the forests grow, without in any way affecting the right and jurisdiction of the individual provinces to administer their own forests in whatever manner they deem fit.
So far as the bill is concerned, I, of course, am denied the opportunity to go into any particulars now, but I would say in summary that the purpose the government has in mind in introducing this resolution on which the bill will be founded is to provide for the conduct of research relating to the protection, management and utilization of the forest resources of Canada and the better utilization of forest products. To that end it will require the establishment and maintenance of laboratories and other necessary facilities for the attainment of these purposes.
We believe too that the federal government will thereby be able to undertake to promote and recommend measures for the encouragement of public co-operation in the protection and wise use of forest resources. We believe that provision should also be made so that the federal government may enter into agreements with the government of any province or with any person for forest protection and management or forest utilization and also for the conduct of research relating thereto, or for forestry publicity or education.
We believe too that there is a field for the federal government in the making of forestry surveys and providing advice relating to the protection and management of forests on lands administered by any department or agency of the government of Canada. Also, where any province desires the co-operation of the federal authorities and requests it, agreements may be arrived at for the protection and management of any of our forests in so far as research is concerned to the end that in co-operation we will be able to provide new opportunities for private enterprise to develop and expand, with the 79951-0-346
Department of Forestry government assuming its responsibility to provide the opportunity through research to bring about utilization in the most beneficial manner and to the maximum extent of these resources which constitute for our country one of its basic strengths and which, if properly conserved in a scientific manner, will permit and assure the perpetuation of this resource for all time to come.
That in summary is the basis upon which I present to the committee, and I trust it will be acceptable, a measure which I feel sure will enable a greater and more diverse use and utilization of these resources which are of such importance to the national economy and to the standard of living of our country.

I will briefly outline the evolution of ideas in connection with the motion before us. Progress has been slow both in Canada and the United States. These ideas have been brought before the public only as the result of the action of a few devoted organizations and individuals. Here are the highlights. The former United States president Teddy Roosevelt sparked the development of conservation policies in that country. The first evidence of action was the establishment of a school of forestry at Yale in 1900. These growing interests developed' in Canada. The first forestry congress was called in 1906 by the governor general of the day and the then prime minister the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. In 1907 we saw the establishment of a school of forestry in Toronto. In 1907 there was established a royal commission on conservation the reports of which may be found in the library. The chairman was the Hon. Clifford Sifton. A member was the father of the present Minister of Justice, the Hon. Frederick Fulton, formerly commissioner of lands in British Columbia, if I remember correctly.
In 1949 we witnessed the introduction of the Canadian Forestry Act as the result of activity on the part of various organizations. Good work has been done under the act with


respect to grants to the provinces for forest inventories which are essential and with respect to the approach to the insect pest question and so on. In 1954 a resources conference was held in Ottawa sponsored by the Canadian forestry association, the agricultural institute of Canada and other organizations. In 1955 the commonwealth conference on resources was held in Canada. Meetings were held in various places in the country and the operation of the industry in various provinces were visited. In 1956 a second resources conference sponsored by the Canadian forestry association and others was held in Winnipeg. In 1959 we had the announcement of the plan for a federal-provincial conference on resources for the future. Today we have before us a resolution to establish a department of forestry.	.
I hope I am not too boastful but I am proud of the part the people of British Col-lumbia played in the development of public opinion and climate with respect to the value of our forests and the need for their conservation and development.

British Columbia was the first province to establish and hold an annual conference on natural resources, which was organized as a result of co-operation among the industry, universities, labour organizations, and the officials of the government department directly concerned. The industry in British Columbia was the first one in Canada by resolution to urge the necessity for a federal-provincial conference to establish a national policy for the conservation of natural resources and it was the first to make representations to the federal government urging the establishment of a department of forestry.

I am very happy to say that last year the first lady to graduate in forestry graduated from the University of British Columbia. I mention this just to indicate that the industry, employees and the people in British Columbia in general have taken a very progressive approach to this problem.
I cannot leave this question without saying that the party to which I belong has also taken a very active part in promoting those ideas and in promoting the general acceptance of the policies that I spoke about previously. From the time the C.C.F. elected members to the legislature in British Columbia-and the hon. member from Vancouver East can tell you all about that-one of the first major policies presented to the legislature on behalf of the C.C.F. was the need for a sustained management policy in the forests of British Columbia and that is our policy today. We all know also that the government of Saskatchewan has done a magnificent job in dealing with the forest resources of that province which, when they took office, were being depleted at a rate which would have meant the disappearance of the major forest resources within the foreseeable future.
Private industry in Canada has also played a very important part in the development of the ideas that are being put forward this afternoon and in the development of research, particularly the pulp and paper industry of this country, and other industry organizations.
For a moment I wish to draw to the attention of the committee the position of Canada in relation to the present world situation so far as the forests are concerned, and to indicate that this is a world problem, and we are dealing with a segment of it in a very intelligent way this afternoon. I intend to quote from a recent report of the food and agriculture organization which indicates how world-wide this problem is and what a responsibility we have not only to the people in Canada but to the world as a whole to conserve our forests. The dispatch is from Rome, dated June 5, 1960, and reads as follows:
Mankind is felling the world's forests dangerously fast, according to the United Nations food and agriculture organization here.
Sixty per cent of forests under exploitation, 3,620,000 acres, are being felled in such a way as to make the future of the world's present timber supply uncertain, declares the FAO's third world forest inventory. And, it adds, because man is not replacing what he takes from nature, the future of about 25 per cent of the forests in use today is in doubt.
The probability of reaping a new crop of timber from a further 35 per cent of the forests now in use is "only reasonably favourable", the FAO says,
Department of Forestry adding that only 40 per cent of the world's forests under exploitation have an assured future through reafforestation.
I just quote from this dispatch to indicate that this is a serious problem for mankind as a whole. We in this group think that Canada is at the turning point. It requires action on the part of the government to give leadership, which I trust the establishment of this department will facilitate, and more co-operation between governments, between conservation minded organizations, between the industry and the people, including the young people in the universities and schools across this country.
In our opinion this new department will face vast and urgent tasks. It also faces a glorious opportunity to do something very substantial and concrete for this industry. It is going to take a dynamic and imaginative approach on the part of the minister who is concerned with the problem and dedication to the cause of the conservation of natural resources and the development of the forest industry.
I suggest there are four major tasks that the new minister will face in this new department. The first will be to promote a successful federal-provincial conference on resources for tomorrow. I think that is necessary in order to make this new department successful and, shall I say, show to the provinces that the result of this department's work will be brought about by co-operation with them without any transgression of their jurisdictions.
The second task is the promotion of the establishment of national principles and policies for the conservation of land, forest, water and other renewable natural resources.
I think the third task is going to be the expansion of research related to the forest industry. I might say at this point that, I was glad to hear that the research work being done by the Department of Agriculture for the forest branch will now be transferred from the Department of Agriculture and come under the jurisdiction of the new ministry. I pay every tribute to the good work being done under the science branch of the Department of Agriculture in this respect. However I and the members of this group for years have contended that it was a somewhat illogical division of responsibility, and we are quite pleased to see this work being brought under the jurisdiction of the new department.
We recognize the excellent work of the forest products laboratory on which I understand we spend approximately $1 million a year at the present time.
Department of Forestry

About $2,500,000 a year while at the same time-and I am glad we do-we spend about $30 million a year on research in agriculture. We need the research in agriculture but I mention these figures to illustrate the gap between the amount spent on research in connection with these two fundamental industries. We recognize the good work being done in research on insect infestation and plant diseases that affect forests. What is required at the present time are more funds for the forest products laboratory to begin with because there is a need for expansion of research owing to the change in the types of equipment and in the type of logging and mechanical operations in the woods. This is the type of research that the forest products laboratory has not had the opportunity to go into to the extent required at the present time because of lack of funds.
In this connection I must mention to the committee that we should not consider ourselves right in the forefront in connection with research so far as the forest industry is concerned. We had a delegation which went to Russia in 1958. It consisted of persons interested in the forest industry and some officials of the forest branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. They had an opportunity to see the operations of the forest industry in the Soviet union with respect to logging operations, milling operations, manufacturing aspects and also with respect to research. I have in my hand a small booklet which was issued by the forest products laboratory of Canada in 1958. It is entitled, "A Canadian's Impressions of Russia's Forest Industries", and is written by J. H. Jenkins who is head of the forest products laboratory and whose good work we all recognize.
I am not going to read extracts from the booklet but it clearly indicates that the Russians are looking forward and are well up with us so far as manufacturing is concerned and possibly with regard to woods operations. However, I have also learned from other sources that they are far ahead of us with respect to the amount of money spent for research in connection with the forest industry. I am not quite sure what the figure is but I understand that they spend several times as many dollars per unit of production on research in the forest industry compared with the amount of money spent by us. I understand they spend close to ten times as much in relation to total production compared with the expenditure by the government of Canada.

In view of the present situation with respect to world markets and the developments in techniques of production I suggest it would be a very good investment for the federal government to spend much larger sums on research related to the forest industry. In addition to expansion of the forest products laboratories we believe there is need for even greater expansion in several very important fields related to forest management into which fields we have not entered to any great extent up to the present time. There should be greatly expanded research into forest management, tree seed production and collection, the development of strains of trees best suited to geographic climate and soil conditions, the suitability of species to site, plant ecology and methods of fire protection.
These are not just my ideas, they are a composite of ideas put forward to the committee by representatives of the forest industry in the various provinces and suggested by various authorities in the universities, by the Canadian forestry association and the Canadian institute of forestry. Therefore I want to stress the need of establishing a program for a great expansion of forest research that immediately envisages the doubling of the professional staff engaged in forest research within the next few years. We think that would be a good investment for the federal government on behalf of all the people of Canada.
Finally, we suggest there is a great opportunity for the federal department of forestry and the minister in charge of the department-a great deal depends on the activity of the minister and his interest in the matter-in the direction of education and publicity. An informed public opinion is required to support a policy of sound forest management. It is very necessary and to a great extent it is now lacking. There are probably few undertakings that have so many amateur advisers whose opinions are often based on sentiment without any knowledge and with little experience. We have got to get the truth and the facts before the Canadian people.
On the other hand, a public consciouness must be developed that the protection of the forests from fire is everyone's responsibility. In that respect I think that in some sections of Canada, particularly the urban areas, the understanding is far less than it should be. The federal government, through its own actions and through the subsidization of properly constituted public information organizations, can help to correct this apparent lack of appreciation on the part of the public of the need for sound, economic management of the forest resource and of the great hazards of forest fires.

In concluding my remarks at this stage I say that co-operation and co-ordination in the development of educational and publicity programs between the federal government, the provincial governments, industry, interested organizations and the schools is one of the tasks that the new minister and department should undertake. Let us mobilize all the people, all the governments, all the agencies, all the organizations that are interested in this problem in support of a national forest policy for Canada, for as the old scripture writer said in Deuteronomy, chapter 20, verse 19, "The tree of the field is man's life".
