Many take the attitude that we have plenty of trees so why worry? This has probably been the reason why we have been so slow in approaching the 79951-0-347
Department of Forestry problem in its proper light. It is probably the reason for the lethargy that has been displayed by the general public and, in some cases, by senior levels of government toward facing the reality that there is a challenge in the field of forest conservation and in preserving the economic solvency of one of our greatest revenue producing basic industries.
Torrents of words are spoken in this house each session about matters that are of infinitesimal importance compared to forestry problems. If one looks through the Hansard for previous years he finds few references to our forest resources and their problems. Agriculture seems to be the predominant interest at all times, and yet the two resources have many common problems and are closely comparative in their economic importance. Canadians seem to be a race of farmers at heart. Certainly one cannot help but come to this conclusion if our parliamentarians represent the thoughts and interests of the people.
I was looking through the proceedings of the 1959 committee of the other place on land use, and it is informative to note that one meeting only was devoted to land use for forestry purposes, despite the fact that for every acre of land in Canada suitable for agriculture there are many acres that could be used for forest production.
I should like to suggest now a few fields to which I feel the new department should give its attention immediately. First among these is the need for greater efforts toward forest fire prevention and control. This is a problem with which we will always be faced. Great efforts and great strides have been made by both provincial and federal forest fire prevention agencies, but there is much to be done yet. Of course, forest fire prevention is largely a matter of public education so far as man-made fires are concerned. However, as long as we have man he will be responsible for a number of forest fires. In addition, of course, we will always have the problem of lightning fires. These often occur in the remote and inaccessible areas and have been responsible for terrific losses. Two years ago we had a terrific loss in the northern part of British Columbia in a very inaccessible area. It was almost impossible to get men and materials in there to control that fire.
The greatest hope for controlling and extinguishing forest fires seems to be in the development and use of aircraft fire control techniques and, perhaps, the development of chemical aids. Much promising technical information is already available, but the cost of experimenting to adapt this information to a practical use is often too high for individual companies and, in many cases, for provinces.

Department of Forestry A number of companies recently banded together in British Columbia to purchase surplus Mars flying boats for use in forest fire fighting. It is an interesting experiment and is being closely watched by everyone all over the world interested in forest fire prevention. These aircraft are capable of carrying several thousand gallons of water and have been equipped for fast reloading. The project is an expensive one, and the companies involved are to be commended for embarking on this venture. Of course, the companies concerned are going to give priority to their own forest holdings. However, if the experiment is successful or shows merit, I suggest that a national aerial forest fire fighting force, adequately equipped and with highly trained personnel, should be an objective of this new department. Such a force could be of material help to the provinces in attaining an objective of a minimum of forest losses through fire.
Emergency fire danger conditions, as a rule, do not extend through all provinces at the same time, and the cost of equipping and maintaining an efficient aerial fire protection unit is beyond the means of most provinces. The federal government derives large amounts of revenue from our forests. It is only right that they should accept a fair share of the cost of their protection.
There is also the question of insect infestation, an ever present threat to our forests. Efforts toward the control of this threat have thus far been directed toward meeting emergency situations only. As a rule a dangerous situation is allowed to build up and become a real emergency before concerted efforts are made to control the threat. I think prevention, in this case, is the sensible course to pursue and I say that should be the policy of this new department. Of course we all know of the work that has been going on for many, many years in the forest products research laboratory, which has made tremendous contributions in the field of forest products design and production.
I believe that one of the primary fields and the field that offers the greatest promise for this department is the field of forestry silvacultural research. We spend annually many millions of dollars on our agricultural experimental stations across Canada. Of course this is as it should be. However, a comparison between these expenditures and those made in forest research is, to say the least, discouraging to anyone who recognizes the importance of the forest industry to our economy.
I think I can best sum up the need for forestry research with a few quotations from eminent authorities. I am going to read a paragraph from the 1959 annual report of


Resources for the Future, Inc., which is a United States organization. Many of the resource problems in the United States are similar to our problems. This report states:
By 2000 our forest lands-
They are referring of course to United States forest lands.
-might well be producing double their present output. New strains of trees can be selected or bred, just as new varieties of crops have been bred, which will be much more productive than the usual ''wild'' strains. Quicker replanting, to obtain a full stand of trees when natural reseeding methods fail or are slow, will speed up output. All sorts of cultural measures are possible; fertilization of forest lands may well become feasible at some future date. Adequate road systems, continuously maintained, will facilitate not only fire control but also disease and insect control. The possibilities of intensive forestry have scarcely begun to be tapped.
Then again in the final report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects reference was made to the same subject. I should like to read a bit of it. Speaking of forestry research, they say:
The logical starting point for such research activities is at the source of the raw material and comes under the heading of "forest management". Stated most simply, it is the object of such management to increase yields in the best and most accessible locations, thus to make possible more intensive operations without impairment of-indeed with improvements to-the preferred stands. The advantages are obvious: reduction of the onerous transportation costs associated with long hauls, and reduction of high labour costs associated with high labour turnover and low productivity. Year-round logging from permanent campsites or town-sites and increased mechanization are the means toward these ends. Control and reduction of forest losses, already referred to, are also a vital part of the management function. Encouragement should be given to tree farming. The farm woodlot generally has the advantages of good location and in addition has a ready labour supply in the farmers themselves. We are not yet at the stage in Canada where we can say simply, "All our forests should be brought under management". The areas involved are too large and much of the area is too remote; the cost burden too high. In order to obtain ample returns for the costs involved, intensive management should be concentrated on the proximate forest areas; in the more remote areas, the emphasis should be on protection with preservation as the primary objective.
There were further references by witnesses before the mines, forests and waters committee in 1958 and Mr. Mahood from British Columbia explained the importance of this type of research. It was also stressed by Professor Love, associate professor of forestry of the University of Toronto at the mines, forests and waters committee meeting last year.
I think this is a most important field of endeavour and one on which the new department should lay the greatest possible emphasis because I think our ability to maintain

our position in world markets in the sale of our forest products will depend to a great extent on forestry research.
Once again may I offer my congratulations to the Prime Minister for the introduction of this motion and assure him that to date I have heard only one person question the advisability of setting up the new department of forestry and that was in the house this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Unlike the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Kootenay West, I cannot speak on this resolution with the degree of expert knowledge they possess. I speak in the light of the important place that the forest industry occupies in the economy of my own riding and that of the province of British Columbia as a whole. It was only necessary to hear the delegation that came before the standing committee on mines, forests and waters last year to realize the pre-eminent position the forest industry holds in the economic life of Canada. It is inherent in this resolution that the government recognizes that place and is prepared to take action that will be of benefit to an industry that sustains so much of the economy of the country and that provides a livelihood for so many Canadians.
Because of the large contribution the forest industry makes to the welfare of the Canadian people I was astonished at the extraordinarily indecisive approach of the hon. member for Laurier this afternoon. I could not help feeling that by taking that indecisive point of view and perhaps, in speaking for his party he had failed to recognize to what degree so much of Canada is entirely dependent on a prosperous and developing forest industry.
In British Columbia there is no need to remind any citizen of his debt to the forest industries or of how much he is dependent on them. If anyone has any doubts he need only refer back to the testimony the British Columbia forest industry gave to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters last year. In the final report of the committee, in paragraph 55, there is an extract from the representations made by the forest industry which, in order to emphasize its case for increased federal government action, states four points:
(1)	The production of forest products is, by a wide margin, Canada's largest industry.
(2)	It is an export industry vital to the national welfare which must meet highly competitive conditions in price and quality on the world market.
(3)	As a natural resource industry it is an industry in which government policies have a decisive role.
(4)	It is an industry with a high employment potential, capable of substantial expansion.
79951-0-347J
Department of Forestry
Of those four points there are two in particular which emphasize the importance of the establishment of a department of forestry in the federal government. First, it is a national resource industry in which government policies have a decisive role. This is not just an observation made by somebody who has come in off the street. It is an observation made by some of the most qualified and highly competent men in the forest industry in Canada.
Second, it is an industry with a high employment potential. In view of the debates that have taken place in the House of Commons during this session and in view of the interest which the hon. member for Laurier and others have taken in this subject of unemployment, here is a justification for the federal government's decision that this industry requires and deserves a department of government to create policies and to give leadership for the development and benefit of an industry with a high employment potential. Not only is it now employing one in every twelve Canadians employed in the production of goods, but there is a further potential that can be exploited. This matter is of the greatest consequence to Canada at the present time. The information I am using is available in the minutes of the mines, forests and waters committee of last year. All of it is available to members of the House of Commons. But my own particular interest lies in the fact that of the forest production in my own riding, and in so many ridings surrounding it, 70 to 75 per cent of it goes into the export market, very largely to the United States. This is a very high proportion of the production of any single industry to be going into the export market and it is a very high proportion of our people who are dependent on the health of our export position for their livelihood. Therefore, when the Prime Minister in his opening remarks mentioned the emphasis of the committee on the requirement for a marketing section, I realize what value could be derived from the creation of this department by the section of the country which I represent and where the export market is of such immense value to an industry that is sustaining a large proportion of the population.
It was also impressive to me to recall that in the testimony before the committee on mines, forests and waters last year submissions of the British Columbia forest industry indicated that Canada's share of the export market had been declining. They pointed out that while the physical volume of sales, particularly in pulp and paper, have been increasing and that the physical volume of

sales proportionately in lumber have been increasing, our percentage share of the available market had decreased.

To
resume the comments I was making, may I point out that the percentage of the Canadian share of the world market has been declining despite the increase in the physical volume of exports, and that this decline has been taking place as world markets have been increasing. We are losing our position, not through a decline in the volume of exports but through a decline in the percentage of the market we have retained.
If such a situation as this exists, and if measures are to be found to assist the industry in Canada to overcome the present difficulties, then a department of government charged with responsibility in this connection seems to me to be the logical and best method of achieving the result desired. I gather that over the years, beyond my experience in this house, requests for government intervention have been made, requests for leadership in the adoption of policies which would provide the Canadian forest industry with an ever-increasing opportunity of expansion and an ever increasing opportunity to make greater employment available so that these greater opportunities might contribute to the general economic welfare of the country.

The contributions made by, among others, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Kootenay West fully recognize the value of the step which the government proposes to take. This is something which has long been needed. If this department is created, if there is imaginative leadership, and if it can bring about the co-ordination of the best work that is being done in the provinces and in industry to contribute to the general welfare of the forest industries of Canada, the benefits which will finally accrue to the people of Canada will be beyond measure.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are only two measures which have been introduced by the government this session which in my opinion have been completely acceptable. One is the measure by which they managed to reach agreement to bring grants to the universities of Quebec, and the other is this present measure. I approve of them both from the party and from a personal point of view.
My constituency probably creates more revenue from forestry than any in Canada since from its watershed come products enough to keep 11 pulp and paper mills going, almost all of whose production goes to the United States market. I know from my own experience of forestry that the industry has looked forward for a long while to a move of this kind in the hope that it may lead to a consolidation and invigoration of our policies in this field.
The qualification mentioned by the previous speaker with regard to imaginative leadership raises one of the most important questions. We all know that cabinet ministers vary in the impact that they make, and I can only appeal to the Prime Minister, since it is within his province to lead in making the selection, that he should give this new department to a minister who can make a real impact upon the industry and upon the country as a whole, including the trade side, the marketing side, the research work and the relationship with the provincial authorities. We need a diplomat; we need a hard driver; we need someone who knows something about the industry, or, if he does not, a man who can get on top of the job in a short time.
I think this is probably going to be one of the fundamental departments in the next decade. If hon. members will look at the report of the royal commission on Canada's production prospects, or at other publications or books on the Canadian economy, they will see that the fundamental factor in our whole future is the forest industry. For that reason I think the government is to be commended on the move it proposes.
Department of Forestry
I do not want to go on any further into the nature of the bill. I will just say this; that in so far as the administration of the department is concerned I suggest to the minister, whoever takes over this portfolio, that he will very quickly need to establish at the head of his civil service a number of young, aggressive people. I say this in no criticism of the members of the present forestry branch, but in general they are not too far away from retirement in so far as both the forestry branch and the forest products laboratory are concerned. I hope this will be one of the young and interesting departments to be in, and I hope that some one will go out and recruit staff if necessary outside the present service to make sure that we have a young, go-ahead group at the head of affairs.
I should also like to suggest that the sooner this department is set up the better, in view of the conservation conference we are holding next year. I think that conference will give the first opportunity for us to judge what the calibre of this department is going to be and what conception this government has of its operations, because if the conference is to be as wide-ranging as has been suggested by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, then the federal department must play a very large part. That conference, it seems to me, will be a proving ground, and I hope by the time it meets next year we shall have a vigorous and, I hope, a young minister in charge of the department and that there will be a relatively new and dedicated civil service leadership.
We are very happy about the bill, and we hope it presages great things for the forest industry in Canada.

Those of us who live on the Alberta prairies are supposed to know very little about trees, but we do know that if we wish to raise a tree on the prairie we have to carry water to it. Those of us who have been here since 1958 as new members have gained some appreciation of the importance of the timber industry in Canada through our association with hon. members from other provinces, and on that basis it seems to me that the introduction of this resolution is most commendable and that the Prime Minister is to be congratulated.
It is not my intention to take the time of the committee except to express one thought -that trees and water, as I indicated in my introductory remarks, are very closely related. We who live in Alberta know something about the east slope of the Rockies and the waters that come from that east slope. We know of the inter-relationship between forestry and irrigation, and between domestic

Department of Forestry water supplies and power development; we know of the problems of irrigation extension, which go back to water, and I would hope that in the next few years-not initially, perhaps, but in the next few years-there may be a widening of the work of the committee of the house in which the new minister will be particularly interested until it becomes what I might term a conservation committee rather than a forestry committee. The hon. member for Laurier this afternoon expressed criticism of this resolution. The hon. gentleman expressed the view that he was for it and that he was against it. As a signature tune he concluded on the note that this could be worked into the Department of Agriculture.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to express my hearty approval of the resolution before the committee at this time. I do not propose to speak in detail because many hon. members have already done so and, frankly, I took advantage of the throne speech debate earlier this year to discuss in detail and substance the question of forestry.
It is with a certain amount of regret that I draw to the attention of the committee the fact that so few hon. members from the provinces of Quebec and Ontario have participated in this debate. With so many hon. members from the west coast addressing themselves to this question the impression could be created that this department will serve primarily, if not solely, the needs and requirements of the forest industry of British Columbia. Nothing could be further from the truth. This industry is first in terms of employment in the whole of our national economy. It represents the greatest volume of export dollars to the nation and has for many years. The well being of forestry generally depends on complete co-operation and understanding between all levels of government and certainly requires, on the federal level, a department which can undertake many programs such as those of a long range scientific research nature which cannot be undertaken by the industry or the provinces at this time.
In stating the importance of this industry to the nations economy I wish to impress most strongly upon hon. members that, while the contribution of the forests to the economy of British Columbia is greater in percentage terms than the contribution our forests make to the economy of the other provinces, it nevertheless represents the greatest earning and employment factor in the economies of Ontario and Quebec as well.

The need for this department is amply demonstrated by the dependence of our lumber markets today on exports to the United States. Many Canadians are not aware of the standards now established by our neighbour to the south with respect to federal housing authority requirements in relation to the standardization of lumber. No agency exists today in Canada which can, in a co-operative way, establish in the Canadian industry national standards which will meet those demanded by our great southern neighbour. Should anything happen to that export potential Canada will dearly suffer.
I was somewhat appalled to hear the distinguished hon. member for Laurier suggest that the forest industry, which is Canada's greatest single employer and export dollar earner, should be dependent upon a federal department such as mines and technical surveys. In saying this I am not in any way being critical of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. For the last three sessions I have had the honour to serve on the committee of mines, forests and waters along with many of my colleagues from British Columbia. It is a self-evident fact that the hon. member for Laurier did not serve on this committee for had he, he would not overlook so many basic requirements of the forestry industry.
It is a fact that forestry operations are far different from mining operations. In the one case you have Canada's greatest recurring, renewable resource. The forests, if forestry is properly practised, with proper scientific guidance, the resource will renew itself. With mining you have an intrinsically different problem. In mining you are extracting a depreciating resource. The basic, fundamental thinking in the operation of the mines department is completely and utterly divorced from the thinking required for the function of a properly constituted forestry department.
I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister on this most worth while measure. I will further say that so far as the economy of this dominion of ours is concerned, if during the term of office of this government no other measure is brought forward, this measure alone will justify the accolade and the support for years to come of the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR CREATION OF NEW DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I, too, am very pleased and wish to congratulate the government upon the setting up of this forestry department. However, I should like to express a fear that I have. I hope that this department will do more for forestry than the mines branch has done for mining. If it does not, I think probably we should leave it the way it is.
Department of Forestry
The forest industry is different from other industries. Hon. members from the west have raised one problem. We in the east have a different problem entirely. We are not so concerned with the renewal of our forests. I keep thinking of the years that I spent in that industry where we were continually told how much reforestation was being done by the companies that were doing the reforestation. Yet as you went through the country you were continually faced with the problem of mills closing down and mills with only a life span of another five or ten years, and no more trees to replace those that had been cut down.
I was very surprised in negotiating with management of particular companies in the white pine industry to find out during the negotiations that they were not particularly interested even in continuing their operations at that time because they said that in another five years they would no longer be operating their mill anyway; that their limits were completely exhausted. I, being naive, as the Canadian people are in many instances, suggested that it only meant starting back where they had originally cut on the old part of their limits. I said that since they had been on the limits for 40 or 50 years the trees in the old areas would have grown up and be ready for cutting. I was informed that it would be 90 or 100 years before there were any trees of commercial value on those limits.
Therefore, I have some doubts when I hear people in this house tell us that reforestation has taken place, or reforestation is being done at a satisfactory rate. That may be true in some sections of the industry but it is certainly not true in the Ottawa valley and in the upper Ottawa. I keep thinking of the Swedish scientist who came out here many years ago. He looked at the white pine industry in the Ottawa valley. He travelled throughout the valley and inspected the industry. When he returned to Sweden he told his people that there was no point in their continuing their lumbering operations; there was no point in their continuing to build toward the future in the lumbering field and in the field of wood products because in Canada we had enough timber to supply the needs of the world in perpetuity.
Well, Mr. Chairman, on the Ontario side of the Ottawa river at the present time you can count the white pine trees growing naturally in the Ottawa valley. Any reforestation that has taken place has been done in the main in areas where one would not expect to see any reforestation at all. The Ottawa valley is denuded completely of the white pine industry which gave to Ontario and to all of Canada the early impetus and

Department of Forestry assisted in the growth that has taken place in this area. The industries that are now in existence are not cutting white pine logs; they are operating mostly in provincial parks or in Quebec Where the rate of cut has not been as great as it has been on the Ontario side of the river.
This department can assist in setting up reforestation. It is all well and good to say that regeneration takes place naturally. These things can be accepted but when you go out into the forests you find that many of the species which are supposed to regenerate themselves do not do so. In Ontario, and particularly in northern Ontario, you can check this at any time. You will fly over vast areas, mile after mile after mile, where there is no green foliage at all and where a tree does not exist.
We shall have to give consideration to the policies which have been in vogue in the last 50 years in relation to our forestry industry. I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister on making this division in the department and setting up this new forestry branch because it has a role to play in Ontario as it has in other parts of Canada. It has a role to play which can only be played if we get started and do something to solve the problems connected with forestry.
In the main, in northern Ontario no reforestation is taking place. Some of the companies do spasmodic replanting, but this is only of recent date. So far as I know, even a company the size of Abitibi does such little reforestation that you can count on your fingers all the trees that they planted 20 years ago. I know of only one small piece of reforestation on the Abitibi limits. There may be more; I may be wrong in saying there are not. To my knowledge the only reforestation is taking place behind a small mill of Abitibi. There is an island behind the mill and 40 or 50 years ago reforestation was practised there as a hobby, and a number of trees of fairly good size are growing, and some are ready for cutting. In the main, mile after mile after mile of the area of Abitibi, an area as large as the British isles, is in this position.
For years and years they cut the trees and did no worrying about the future generations who were to depend on those areas. Over 50 years ago, and probably a few years before that, when the early lumbering industry, the early sawmills and loggers, went into Timiskaming, the area was covered with white pine, and beautiful stands of timber they were. Because this was a profitable enterprise, because it had something that the west did not, you could go into northern Ontario and homestead for the first years. You cut the trees, you sold the lumber off the land,


you sold the pulpwood, and you as a homesteader were able to make a living in those areas by utilizing the trees in that way. Many homesteaders did that. They cut all through northern Ontario; they cut over land that had been logged by large logging operators previously. They cut the lumber and they cut the pulpwood that had been left and they were able to open up the land and to clear a great deal of the area.
This operation was carried out in years gone by, especially north of Cochrane and up through the great clay belt of that area. It was found afterwards that much of the land that had been cleared, after they had taken off the first few crops, was not suitable for agriculture and should not have been turned into agricultural land. Now areas such as these lie abandoned. No trees are growing on them except tag alders and willows. It has no commercial value and no value as agricultural land. In a small way the Ontario government has gone into that area and established a survey group to ascertain what should be done with the land. It would seem to me that they will probably finally decide to put it back into forest by planting the type of trees that were originally there and that we will grow trees like we grow grain and other products. At the end of the year we will know how much we have for the years to come and how much reforestation must be done to take care of the growing markets we will have.
Only last week end we had a flash flood in Timiskaming. I am informed that creeks and farm lands were flooded where there is never any water except in the spring. Some of these little creeks, which are completely dry all summer and have hay growing in them that is used for pasture purposes, had seven to eight feet of water in them. I understand that the water crossed the road in front of my house and took out a six foot culvert. It cut a 20-foot path through the roadway and carried a steel culvert, not corrugated iron, over a wire fence and down the creek. Flash floods of this type usually do not bother us. I do not remember such flood conditions even in the spring.
This department is going to have to give consideration to the problems that have been caused by the elimination of the forests. In lake Timiskaming and the Ottawa river not only in my area but right outside the parliament buildings we are continually having flood problems and later in the year there is not enough water power to operate our industrial and hydro installations. It seems to me that one thing this department must concern itself with is reforestation in order

to protect the watersheds because we depend on the water being available for commercial, hydro and pleasure uses.
The provincial governments have done something along this line, as have the municipalities, but so far the federal government has done very little. I was surprised to find there is a survey team in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I had the opportunity of flying to the mari-times with one of the officials and he told me about the work that is being done in the maritimes with respect to assessing the potentialities of the watersheds in that area. I think the Canadian people generally should be told that this service is available and it is time that people like those I represent in northern Ontario found out what the potentiality is, what reforestation is necessary to protect the watersheds and how we can overcome some of the problems we have created for ourselves by eliminating forests completely, particularly in those areas where we have no trees and have not been able to make any use of the land.
Reforestation in order to serve the purpose will have to be planned to meet the needs of the particular area. I am sure that these needs will be assessed and leadership will be given by this department. In my opinion the reforestation that has taken place on the provincial level has been spasmodic. I have seen better reforestation that has been done by some of the old municipalities that decided 20, 30 or 40 years ago to plant trees on land that had been repossessed for non-payment of taxes. Around Kemptville and in Dufferin, Wellington and other communities you can see much better reforestation programs than anywhere in northern Ontario where it is natural for the people to assume that reforestation is an industry and not just a pastime.
I am told that reforestation will pay off if governments go into it and that there are municipalities adjacent to New York where the citizens live free of taxes because of the revenue received through reforestation done on a continuous basis over the years. I think the Canadian people want to leave their children, not with the heritage in the forest industry that was left to us but with the same situation that prevailed when our grandfathers and great-grandfathers came to this country. The forests are a renewable resource. They are not like mines where the natural resource is taken out of the ground and can never be replaced. If we use common sense we can have more trees and a bigger forest industry in Canada in the future than we have today.
I think this department will give great leadership with respect to a problem that
Department of Forestry also plagues us in relationship to pollution and other ills suffered, not only because of waste dumped into waters by sawmills and paper companies but other pollution. I think this matter will certainly have some relationship to the department of forestry if it is going to be successful and fulfil the needs of the Canadian people.
In setting up the department I hope the government also has in mind the problem of research into the forest industry and the marketing problem. I have represented for a number of years workers in the lumber industry and I am well aware of the problems facing the workers and those that face the industry with relation to markets over which they have no control. We in Canada have a limited opportunity to expand our markets beyond those that are traditional. When our traditional markets in England and on the continent were affected by stiff competition from Russia we were forced to send our products to eastern Canada and to the south. They entered markets that were highly competitive and in many cases we were not able to compete. We also found great difficulty when western producers undertook a crash program whereby they shipped lumber billed to Chapleau, for example, and other points in northern Ontario without any sales having been made. They shipped this lumber in bankrupt lots and it had to be cleared out at any price to meet the demurrage costs at the distribution point. Eastern producers had to compete with this bankrupt stock and this in turn created havoc in our traditional markets in eastern Canada.
The western producers are not to be blamed to any extent because they were faced with a difficult problem in the face of imports from Japan and other countries that were competing on a basis that we could not meet. They had the ability and the research knowledge to develop veneers 10 to 20 times as effective as ours. They had the methods and the machinery to cut veneers 10 to 20 times as thin as ours. They were able to import not only from other countries but from Canada the logs they required, particularly birdseye maple, and to return the veneers to Canada at a price with which our producers were not able to complete.
Therefore I hope the department will give serious consideration to doing research on an industry-wide basis so that all segments of the industry will be able to take advantage of the latest developments in technology. Many of our small mills and plants are not able to compete because of the advances in technology today and they are going to have to have assistance to modernize their mills

Department of Forestry and to develop procedures and methods of production which they are not now capable of undertaking.
In closing, I should like to point out that many of our mills are operating at a very low rate of efficiency. They are operating on an efficiency of 35 per cent to 40 per cent. These mills are in competition with mills in countries like Sweden and Norway which are operating on an efficiency of 80 per cent or 90 per cent. While many of our mills are only taking the choice cuts from sawmill logs and the choice grades of lumber, the mills in these other countries are bringing in the whole tree and processing everything but the leaves. We are operating in a manner that leaves waste wood in the forest and have not been taking full advantage of the abundant growth we have had in this natural resource.
I believe this is a very opportune time for this government to set up the new department. I feel that a great deal of co-operation can be obtained from labour, from management and from conservationists throughout the country to the end that every year Canada will become richer in these various products and our forest industry will contribute more and more to our general economy.

I wish to make a few observations on this resolution, inasmuch as I happened to have the honour of chairing the committee which brought in the report about which we have heard so much today. We have heard representations from many hon. members of that particular committee who contributed a great deal to the preparation of the final report and who knew a great deal more about the problems of the forest industry than the chairman. I was very pleased today to hear the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay West and others in his party who are supporting this resolution. I am going to have something to say before I close about the remarks made by one of the Liberal speakers who did not happen to be a member of that committee.
I do appreciate-and I am sure the members who were on that committee and who contributed so much to the final report must be gratified-the commendation that has been given the work of this particular committee. I do not recall, during my experience in this house even as an opposition member, when a resolution received so much commendation on such a high level. It is not often that the setting up of a new department of government receives the support that this move has received today. It does involve the necessary expenditures connected with a new department and its staff.
I believe, that as chairman of that particular committee I am expressing the opinion

of every member of the committee when I commend the government for taking action so quickly, less than eight months after the report was submitted. I am sure that the reaction throughout the country will be most favourable to the government because of the importance of the forest industry to the economy of Canada. I should like to say to hon. members who were not members of that committee that all they need to do to become impressed with the work of the committee is, for instance, to read the list of witnesses who appeared before the committee. It is no wonder that those who were members of the committee spoke so effectively. We did not take one glance at the problems of the forest industry. We had some 40 or 50 representations made to the committee and the various witnesses were given all the time they required to make those representations. In the main, they were all sound and very effective.
I do not intend to repeat what has been said today by other speakers on this resolution. Needless to say, this is one of the most important industries in the Dominion of Canada, and I think it will continue to be so in spite of the increased demand for our oil and gas. It is a renewable industry. It is not like mining. In 1958 the total exports of wood products were close to $1.5 billion or about 29.36 per cent of our exports in that year. The thing that amazed me was that the previous government, with all their administrative staffs of technicians and advisers, did not realize the importance of the forest industry to this country. The industry was allowed to wobble along like a lame duck for many years without proper guidance. In my opinion the press of this country will react favourably to the establishment of a forestry department because of the importance of this industry. There are other matters which I believe could be incorporated within this department, but I will not deal with those at the moment.
As I said a moment ago, I do not intend to repeat what was said earlier. Many of the briefs presented to the committee came from British Columbia because the forest industry is of great importance to that particular province. We did receive some representations from Quebec and Ontario as well as other parts of Canada. I should like now to quote from page 1175 of the committee report where it states:
Your committee strongly recommends consideration of steps which would widen the scope of the forestry branch, increasing its status in such a way that a deputy minister would be in direct charge. The fact that such a status, comparable to that of a department does not exist now reflects a lack of appreciation of the importance of the forest industries to Canada, in the past, now, and in the future.

I suggest that is a very important conclusion to be drawn by any committee. When we made this report we made it in the way we thought it should be made. We were given an assignment and this is the report that was tabled in this house. The report contains other recommendations to which I could refer, but I shall not do so at this time.
I must say, in conclusion, that this particular industry is so important to our economy, and will continue to be so important that I am highly appreciative of the government's move to establish a separate administration to take care of the forest industry in this country. As I recall, there were 27 Conservatives on that committee, seven Liberals and one C.C.F. The C.C.F. member made an excellent contribution without any doubt. When we made our report it was unanimously adopted. In view of the fact that many of the witnesses who appeared before the committee suggested that a new department of forestry should be established, and in view of the fact that every member of the committee wanted the forestry branch to have a higher status, I was amazed this afternoon to hear a most distinguished Liberal member, one who is recognized all over this country-I refer to the hon. member for Laurier-

Supply-Transport AFTER RECESS
The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

When the committee rose last night I was just warming up in my description of the mess we had got ourselves into on a national basis with regard to our transportation, a position where we are subsidizing our railways in almost every way possible while at the same time subsidizing transport on our highway.
A further point we must take into consideration is the terrific loss of life we experience on our railroad crossings. I realize that efforts have been made to overcome this danger, particularly in the past number of years, and that millions of dollars have been spent recently in an effort to eliminate some of the hazards which present themselves in connection with railroad crossings over our highways. Unfortunately as fast as we eliminate some of these dangerous crossings our efforts are offset by the increase in road traffic and we find that the situation is no better than it was in spite of the millions of dollars which have been spent.
Another thing we have to take into account is the terrific loss of life caused by the presence of big transports on our highways cluttering our roads. Any motorist who has had the experience of driving over roads where these big boxcars block the traffic, travelling at high speeds downhill and at very slow speeds uphill, will understand what I have in mind. A frustrated driver in a desperate effort to get by takes a chance, pulls out and another fatal accident occurs. This is no criticism of the drivers of the transports because I think that but for the ability and courtesy of transport drivers in general the toll of human life would be greater than it is. However, the present situation emphasizes the fact that our highways are no place for boxcars.
Today we see another situation developing. The railway companies are getting into this field of transport. They are buying out the transport companies and then they find themselves in the fortunate position of being able to make a profit on their road operations and obtain a subsidy with respect to their railroads. As I pointed out the other day, the only reason why they can make a profit on their transport undertakings is because we are subsidizing transport also by building the roads for them.
It is no use hon. members who support the government pointing out, as they have done before, what a wonderful example of private enterprise the C.P.R. represents and comparing it favourably with the C.N.R. Looking back at the history we find that the story
[The Deputy Chairman.]
does not stand up to examination because the Canadian taxpayers have subsidized the C.P.R. in the way of grants, land grants and so on far more than they have subsidized the C.N.R.
What we need in this country, and what we need more urgently every day is an overall transport policy, something we have not had up to the present time. We must have some leadership from the federal government in order that we may be able to make the best use of our railways and our air and road services.
Today we find that men are being laid off by the railways by the thousand after having 30 or 35 years of experience. They have no training which would fit them for any other job but despite this they are just being turned out on the labour market. Many of these men are in no position to afford to train themselves for other jobs because they have to look after families and cannot spare the money necessary to train themselves to take up other occupations. They find that after 20, 25 or 30 years of service there is no more use for their skills and they have no qualifications to take other jobs.
We have proof in the past that the government can do a job. At the end of the last war hundreds of thousands of ex-servicemen were trained to fit themselves into society on their return from the services. But hon. members must realize that some provision was made for the families of these men, if they had families, so they themselves could obtain the training which was necessary before they could become re-adapted to the needs of society. The result was that not only did they benefit by equipping themselves with new skills but the country as a whole benefited by the training they had received.
I suggest that the time has come when the government should take a close look to determine whether it should not take over both the transcontinental railroads and whether it might not be in the interest of all concerned for them to find out in which areas it is most economical to use rail and which areas it might be more successful and more economical to tear up those tracks and turn them into transport roads, thus taking the heavy transport vehicles off our highways. There is one thing that should be kept in mind: if the government should begin such a program it must accept its responsibility for training people to make the necessary change, and avoid the dislodgement which is occurring today across the country from coast to coast. Let us think for one moment of the savings which could be made in connection with the upkeep and maintenance of our highways once

these big transports have been taken off the road and put on a road which they maintain and look after themselves.
I recall talking not too long ago to an old foreman from the town of Foleyet which at one time was a railway centre of considerable importance. As time went on and automation took over the job this man had was discontinued, but he had enough seniority; he was able to bump into another job. He bumped right up to yard foreman, and then they abolished the yard, and after 32 years he was turned out on the street with a very small pittance of a pension. After 32 years he was considered of no use in the line of work which he had carried on all his life.
If this over-all transport policy is undertaken and put into effect it may not mean the dislodgement that some people fear it would mean. The car shops could be converted into transport garages. The express and freight people could transfer to handling the freight and express now handled by the railways. There would be no need for a change in the personnel we have in this field. This is something the government should take into consideration. It is time for bold leadership in this field. The government should take the lead in studying this field and implementing policies that would lead to greater efficiency and economies. The government could create order out of the chaos that now exists. Perhaps most important of all it could give those employed in this field some idea of what is ahead and not leave them waiting as they are now from day to day to see when the axe is going to fall.
Mr. Chairman-
Oh, no, not again. Lay off, old boy.

I see that the hon. member for Vancouver South is interrupting. I thought I would have had the pleasure of hearing from him at this time. I heard it rumoured that his name was on the list. Since it is not, I am forced to speak on this item because my remarks would probably be out of order on a detailed item.
I do not intend to cover the ground I covered last night but I wish to elaborate on what I said last evening.
For all practical purposes the railway companies have become a law unto themselves in their operations and in their abandonment and curtailment of essential services. I said last night that the board of transport commissioners have shut their eyes to the needs of the public and are passing in a wholesale manner the applications of the railways for reductions of service. Our railway facilities
Supply-Transport
are in great danger of being torn down by the very people who are managing the companies. It is a shame that thousands of railway employees are being summarily dismissed after 25 or 30 years of service with no visible means of support. The minister may not consider this a serious matter. I do not think he does. The hon. gentleman has done nothing to relieve the situation. I feel it is a blot on the record of our country that thousands of employees are being put out on the street after a lifetime of service in their occupations.
We have asked the government to take action but the minister pleads that he is powerless, that the management of the C.N.R. is beyond his control or influence. The minister alleges that he has consideration for the hardship that results to these employees but states that after having discussed the question with the C.N.R. nothing has happened. The hon. gentleman alleges, too, that the C.N.R. management is sympathetic to the situation of these employees. They have a strange way of showing sympathy. I think the management has one object in mind and that is to curtail services, bring about so-called modernization as rapidly as possible and to look solely at the balance sheet of the company without any thought whatever to the welfare and suffering of the people who worked for the railway company.
If the minister did not agree with the policy he would change the management of the C.N.R. If the minister disagrees with the policy that is what should be done. The minister, of course, agrees with the policy. The president of the C.P.R., the president of the C.N.R. and the minister are co-operating in what is taking place.
Earlier this day we took steps to continue the freeze on freight rates. This is interference with the railways and the way in which they receive part of their revenue. The government has gone so far in its interference with the railway companies that it has announced a policy to the effect that there will be no further increases in freight rates pending the report of the royal commission. When it comes to a question of freight rates the government interferes directly but when it comes to the welfare of the employees the government refuses to interfere and allows this deplorable condition to continue. The minister and the government take a cruel and callous attitude toward the employees of the railway companies.
I suggest to the minister that for a period of time there should be a freeze in the staff of the railways. There should be a halt to the dismissals now taking place. I believe there are good arguments for putting this forward at this time. We have decided as

Supply-Transport
a parliament that there shall be a freeze on freight rates pending the report of the royal commission inquiring into this question. I suggest there is need now for a royal commission to inquire into the operations of the railway companies as they affect the livelihood and welfare of their employees. The present royal commission investigating freight rates could be reconstituted on completion of its task and be instructed to inquire into the operations of the railway companies as they affect their employees and the public services. We are witnessing wholesale dismissals of employees and a sharp curtailment of services. The public have a right to a full inquiry into what is being done.
Rumour has had it-and the rumour has found its way into the public press-that there is likely to be a curtailment in the present transcontinental passenger service of the two major railways. This kind of rumour going around further demoralizes the employees. This kind of rumour does nothing to build passenger confidence in those railway services. If the railway companies of this country had embarked on a deliberate policy of curtailing and discontinuing further passenger service in this country, then they would have been following their policy very successfully in recent years because apparently this must be what is in their minds when they talk of the discontinuance of those main transcontinental passenger runs.
With all these problems it is important that a halt be called to any further curtailment of service and any further dismissal of employees. In the light of the current unemployment situation in Canada I say it is of no help to our nation to dismiss countless employees of railway companies merely to have them added to the unemployed rolls in our nation. Until such time as this whole situation is clarified I feel that such a freeze in employment levels on the railways is a just thing. I would ask the minister to give consideration to this proposal; I would ask him to make some comment on it and say whether the government would consider the suggestions that I have put forward, to consider a royal commission or some other appropriate study into the policy being followed by the railway companies in this country with particular emphasis on the need to maintain essential railway services for the public and to protect the welfare of company employees.
With respect to a freeze as far as the present personnel of the railways is concerned, I do not have in mind an arbitrary rule that would force the railway companies to maintain their employment levels at the current rate. Such an order, in my opinion, should allow for normal retirement of employees and,

therefore, for a normal or a regular reduction in staff at this rate if this seems desirable from the standpoint of the railway companies. This would be a brake on the wholesale dismissal of employees.
Every few days members of parliament get communications from sections of railway workers across this country, telegraph operators, workers in the car shops, whether they be in Winnipeg, Montreal, London or in some other part of the nation, complaining that their jobs are in jeopardy, that there have been wholesale dismissals and that they are in a very uncertain state of employment because they do not know from one day to the next when their jobs may end. I ask the minister to make some further comment on this question and to hold out, if he can, some hope to the railway employees of this country that these wholesale dismissals will not be continued, and that the type of agreement which has given some stability of employment to the firemen for a period of time may be considered for other sections of railway employees.
Some members may argue that what I am saying would increase or maintain the cost of railway operations, therefore it is a disservice to the users. I do not think we need to play one off against the other. Parliament has acted to protect the public against further increases in freight rates at this time. I think that parliamentary action to protect employees who have spent their lives working for those companies would be an appropriate parallel action at this time.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee was discussing this vote on Friday, June 10, I spoke of the injury which had been inflicted on my home town of Cornwall through the closing of the Cornwall canal, and the hon. member for Laurier immediately rose to reply to me and directed his reply almost entirely to the question of pollution. His reply contained a number of errors and I feel I must rise again to offer my reply to him. He cited certain legislation and certain treaties which I have subsequently taken a hard, long look at, and I wish to inform the committee at the outset that it is not for any personal reason that I rise on this occasion but because, as I shall presently show, expenditures of large sums of money without any justification in either substance or law were made at that time.
First, let me refer to another matter which I should like to correct. Last night the minister commented, I believe, that the report of January, 1951, of the St. Lawrence seaway authority on the economic prospects was laid before the house by Mr. Howe. I can find no evidence of that report having been

made public. In fact, Mr. T. M. Bell filed a notice of motion for the production of this report on June 2, 1954, and as far as I can determine, that was refused.
To get back to the other matter of legislation, may I call the attention of the committee to two sentences in the speech by the hon. member for Laurier. He said, and I quote from page 4785 of Hansard of June 10:
In 1951 an application was made by the government of Canada and the government of the United States to the international joint commission for the development of power in the international section at Cornwall. At that time the Canadian government agreed to build all the canals on the Canadian side of the line.
Now those applications to the international joint commission were not made in 1951; they were made on June 30, 1952. It is important to get that date correct. The hon. member for Laurier should remember it quite well. He was the minister of transport at that time, and he went down to Washington in order to be present at the signing of that application and also at the signing of the note of the Canadian government by the Canadian ambassador to the United'States, Mr. Hume Wrong, to the United States government on the very same day.

The hon. member for Laurier may have had some share in the completion of those negotiations which led to the signing of those Canadian documents, I do not know, I was not there. He has never told the house a single word about those negotiations; he has never offered any explanation of the extraordinary character of this Canadian note. A few moments later the hon. member for Laurier went on to say:
At that time there was an agreement-
By which he obviously meant July and August, 1954. I continue:
-between Canada and the province of Ontario whereby Ontario was to build and maintain 14-foot navigation facilities. When this agreement was brought about there was, therefore.-

-no longer any obligation on the part of the province of Ontario to fulfil that covenant.
The hon. member for Laurier is also a member of the legal profession and perhaps for this reason I should be very careful to refer to him as the hon. and learned member for Laurier. I have always understood it to be a most binding obligation on the part of members of the legal profession when

making reference to a statute to make such reference complete and accurate.
What did the hon. and learned member for Laurier do? He referred to the Canada-On-tario agreement of December 3, 1951, and here again I emphasize the date. That agreement related to the development of the power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river. That agreement was ratified by the International Rapids Power Development Act which was passed and made law before the end of the same month, December 1951, and the full text of that agreement is appended as a schedule to the provisions of this act. The hon. and learned member for Laurier should be well acquainted with the terms of both the agreement and the act because as minister of transport at that time he introduced the bill and piloted it through this house. I shall now read article II of that agreement, omitting some incidental words. It reads:
Canada will do all in its power ... to obtain the approval of the international joint commission ... of works to develop the power resources of the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river to be undertaken by Ontario concurrently with the undertaking of complementary works by an appropriate authority in the United States of America, in accordance with the plan known as the "Controlled Single Stage Project..containing the features described in the annex to this agreement with such modifications as may be agreed upon herein or by Canada and Ontario.
Now I come to the annex of the agreement in which the main features of the project for power development are recited. I find as feature number (7) the following:
The necessary works to permit the continuance of 14-foot navigation on the Canadian side around the control dam and from the pool above the Long Sault dam to connect with the existing Cornwall canal.
Thus far the hon. and learned member for Laurier and I are in complete agreement, I trust. I am especially grateful to him for his acknowledgement in his speech of June 10 which I have just quoted that this obligation on the part of Ontario to make provision for the continuance of 14-foot navigation was still binding upon Ontario in August, 1954.
Now let me go further into the Canada-Ontario agreement of December 1951, much further than the hon. and learned member for Laurier went. In article XI of the agreement, which is quite a lengthy article, Ontario undertook to give all necessary assistance to the government of Canada toward the construction of a deep waterway on the Canadian side of the international rapids section. Article XII of the agreement I must, however, quote in full.
If the construction by Canada of the locks and works mentioned in article XI-

Supply-Transport
That is to say, the locks and works of a deep waterway on the Canadian side of the river.
-renders unnecessary the construction by Ontario of the works required to permit the continuance of 14-foot navigation as described in paragraph seven of the annex to this agreement, Ontario will pay to Canada a part of the cost of such locks and works equivalent to the cost of the works that would have been required to be constructed by Ontario to permit the continuance of such 14-foot navigation.
Upon the basis of the unit cost levels of December 1950, the cost of new provision for the continuance of 14-foot navigation around the control dam at Iroquois would be about $1 million, and the cost of similar provision at Cornwall of about $16 million, a sum total of a little more than $17 million in all.
Now I come to a point about which I am considerably perplexed. Section 2 of the International Rapids Power Development Act, 1951, reads as follows:
The agreement dated the 3rd day of December, 1951, between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Ontario is approved on behalf of and is binding on the government of Canada and all things to be done by virtue thereof are approved and authorized.
Section 5 reads:
This act shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation.
The necessary proclamation to bring the act into force was not in fact issued until May 18, 1953, and it brought the act into force on May 20, 1953.
Can we say, then, that the act was in force on that most important day to which I have already called attention, June 30, 1952, the day of signature of the Canadian application to the international joint commission and of a Canadian note to the United States government, the day of one of the felicitous visits to Washington of the minister of transport? I And it hard to say whether the act was in force at that time. Yet since it had never been amended before it was proclaimed I find it even harder, very much harder, to say that it was not.
Now I come to the documents that were signed on June 30, 1952, four in all, two by the government of Canada and two by the government of the United States. Two of these documents were applications to the international joint commission by the two governments, on behalf of their power developing entities, for permission to develop the power of the international rapids section in accordance with the controlled single stage project. The Canadian application further declared that the government of Canada would construct, maintain and operate all such works as might be necessary to provide and maintain a deep waterway between the
[Mr. Campbell (Stormont).j
port of Montreal and lake Erie, and that such a deep waterway would be provided as nearly as possible concurrently with the completion of the power development works. The application from the government of the United States declared that it was filed with the understanding on the part of the United States that the government of Canada would engage in this work.
Here we have, then, an undertaking by Canada and an understanding by the United States that the deep waterway would be carried through the international rapids section on the Canadian side. And upon that undertaking and that understanding, the recital in each application of the main features of the work included the following provision:
(g) Navigation facilities-provision will be made for the continuance of 14-foot navigation throughout the international rapids section during the construction period.
That is to say, that upon the completion of a 27-foot deep waterway on the Canadian side, this provision of 14-foot navigation would cease. That would seem sensible enough. I think the hon. and learned member for Laurier will agree with me in this. Then, under the terms of the Canada-Ontario agreement of December 3, 1951, which the hon. and learned member for Laurier in his then incapacity as minister of transport helped to negotiate, the provision of article XII, which pledged Ontario to pay to the government of Canada the sum of $17 million dollars or more, would come into effect. That is what the agreement, which was ratified by acts both of parliament and of the legislature of Ontario would seem to require as a simple, straightforward matter of law.
Now I come to the substance, the astonishing substance, of the note that was signed on behalf of the government of Canada in Washington on June 30, 1952, and was presented to the government of the United States on the very same day. The note first stated that it appeared impossible to obtain congressional approval in the near future for United States participation in the construction of deepwater navigation facilities in the international rapids section and that, in consequence, the Canadian government has, with parliamentary approval, committed itself to provide and maintain whatever additional works may be required to allow uninterrupted 27-foot navigation between lake Erie and the port of Montreal. It then proceeded to inform the United States government of two points on which, so it stated, the Canadian government is now prepared to agree. These are points of such cardinal importance that, for

the sake of the record, I find myself compelled to quote them in full. They read:
(a)	that the amount to be paid to Canada, as specified in the agreement of December 3, 1951, between Canada and Ontario, in lieu of the construction by the power developing entities of facilities required for the continuance of 14-foot navigation, be excluded from the total cost of the power project to be divided between the Canadian and the United States power developing entities, in consideration of the fact that the actual replacement of 14-foot navigation facilities will be rendered unnecessary by reason of the concurrent construction of the deep waterway in Canada, and
(b)	that the authority to be established pursuant to the provisions of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act, chapter 24 of the Statutes of Canada, 1951 (second session), contribute $15 million towards the cost of the channel enlargement which the power developing entities must undertake in the St. Lawrence river, as set out in paragraph 4 of the annex to the Canada-Ontario agreement of December 3, 1951, and in section 8 of the applications to the international joint commission, in consideration of the benefits which will accrue to navigation through such channel enlargement.
In short, the Canadian government, by these two concessions, surrendered an asset, an obligation due to it, of at least $17 million and accepted an obligation of $15 million. This was a sacrifice without any authorization or justification, of a sum of more than $28 million, a sum that would be more than sufficient to erect two new government printing bureaus on top of the one that is already there.
A note in reply, signed by the secretary of state of the United States and delivered to the Canadian ambassador in Washington on June 30, stated, first, that, and I quote:
My government approves the arrangement set forth in your note-
That is to say, Canadian construction of the deep waterway on the Canadian side of the international rapids section, and agreed to the two financial concessions offered in the Canadian note, repeating them in the identical words which I have read. According to the significant word in the International Rapids Power Development Act, 1951, an agreement between Canada and Ontario was already in effect and was binding on the government of Canada, and all things to be done by virtue thereof are approved and authorized. Upon a reading of the act, the national government was bound by that very law to hold Ontario to its obligation of payment. Since the act did not, perhaps, take effect in any way until it had been proclaimed, it might be argued that the national government was still free in June, 1952 to come to any terms with the United States government that it might like. The act was, as I mentioned before, proclaimed in force on May 18, 1953.
Supply*-Transport
It would, of course, have been possible for the government to regularize this agreement with the United States either before or after the date of proclamation by the passage of an appropriate amendment to the act. But nothing of the sort was ever done and, accordingly, I submit to the committee that the obligation of Ontario to provide for the continuance of 14-foot navigation through the dikes at Cornwall and to pay the cost of construction of a lock for 14-foot navigation at Iroquois is still in force. The legislation creating this obligation has never been rescinded or modified.
I would go even further than this, by reminding the committee that there exists a common law public right of navigation of the waters of the St. Lawrence river and, by the Department of Transport Act, a statutory right of navigation of the Cornwall canal, with a specific duty laid upon the Minister of Transport to make provision for the exercise of that right.
I come now to the other obligation that Canada assumed, the obligation to be carried by the seaway authority to pay $15 million to the power developing entities as a contribution to the costs of channel enlargement. First let me call attention to the exact words of the undertaking. They are that the authority shall contribute $15 million toward the cost of channel enlargement which the power developing entities must undertake. It is not a payment for any additional channel enlargements, it is a payment for some part of the work that would have to be done anyway to ensure the development of power, no matter whether the deep waterway would be built or not.
I know it may be argued that in spite of the wording of this second Canadian concession the provision of deep water navigation would in fact necessitate some additional channel enlargement at additional expense. I propose, therefore, to meet this argument in advance. The international joint commission held hearings on the Canadian and United States applications in various places. At the hearing in Albany, New York, on September 3, 1952 a representative of the United States corps of engineers presented an estimate for the cost of the channel enlargements required for a development for power alone, without any provision for deep-water navigation, at $71,867,000. This was on the basis of unit cost levels of December, 1950. A corresponding Canadian estimate put the cost of the appropriate channel enlargements at the still higher figure of over $82 million. I challenge anyone who is acquainted with the details of the estimates for the cost of an all-Canadian seaway to put the costs of the necessary

Supply-Transport
channel enlargements in the international rapids section at any higher figure than that.
Thus far I have tried to show just this, that the first of these two concessions by Canada was a contravention of a national law, and the second unwarranted in fact. But what should be said about them as obligations binding upon Canada in relation to the United States? The Canada of June 30, 1952, informed the United States of its intention to proceed to the construction of the deep waterway all by itself, and the reply of the United States declared its agreement with that intention. As I said before, there was a Canadian undertaking and a United States understanding, and both the Canadian concessions rested upon this reciprocal proffer and acceptance. In fact, however, Canada has not by itself constructed an all-Canadian seaway. In consequence these two concessions, as formal commitments to the United States, simply fall to the ground. It is possible, since Canada did build one lock in the international rapids section at Iroquois that some alternative concessions to the United States, on a very much smaller scale, might be negotiated instead. Certainly, for my own part, I see not the slightest reason even for this.
The hon. and learned member for Laurier seems to take some pride in the fact that a concrete structure has been inserted in the line of dikes at Cornwall in preparation, as he put it, for future 27-foot facilities on the Canadian side. I have described that structure as a concrete wall 80 feet high. This is exactly what it is. I think the hon. and learned member for Laurier, who seems anxious to claim at least a share of the credit for it, should actually feel nothing but shame. In fact, he is entitled to all the credit for it. He was born and brought up in Cornwall. He has been trained as a lawyer; he has practised in Cornwall and surely he, of all people in this house, should be most keenly aware of the statutory right of navigation through the Cornwall canal. He, of all members in this house, should be the very last to procure the destruction of that right by even thoroughly legal means, yet he, in fact, of all people has deliberately approved of such destruction and that by wrongful means.
