Under date of June 17 I understand the Minister of Transport received a telegram from the Canadian director, E. C. Sims, with regard to a stoppage of box car deliveries of grain to the port of Vancouver.
I asked a question on that matter and I want to thank the Minister of Transport for his co-operation. He asked me to see him in his office to discuss the matter and he made an appointment for me with the chairman of the board of transport commissioners. I want to say that the co-operation I have received on this most important matter from the minister and from the board of transport commissioners is something for which I am grateful. It is the greatest co-operation I have ever received during any of my time here in Ottawa. Of course, as you know, Mr. Chairman, the best way in which to get things done is to give compliment where compliment is due. I want to say that I have received from the minister and from the chairman of the board of transport commissioners the finest of cooperation. I understand that everything is now functioning very well and that grain is now going through the port of Vancouver.
However, the point I want to raise is this. This entire story is an intriguing one in that it appears that there was a stoppage in the shipping of grain to Vancouver because of reports that there was an impending strike in Vancouver. All my information shows that there could not have been an impending strike in Vancouver because the two unions concerned had gone to federal conciliation. To the best of my knowledge no federal conciliation award has yet been made. Therefore up to the present moment under the law both federally and provincially there is no impending strike.
The point I want to raise with the Minister of Transport is this: I have here a photostatic copy of a column published in the Vancouver Sun on June 8. The Minister of Transport did not know of this situation until he received a wire on June 17, and I know, because of the courtesy granted to me by the chairman of the board of transport commissioners, that they did not know about that on June 21,

and yet I read in this photostatic copy from the Vancouver Sun the headline:	"Strike

Threat of strikes by two waterfront unions is causing concern in the continuing drop off in grain shipments through British Columbia ports, Vancouver port manager Captain B. D. L. Johnson said today.
Then there are a number of statements which are not in quotation marks. I want to draw the attention of the minister to the last paragraph in this report from the Vancouver Sun which says:
Captain B. D. L. Johnson summed up the situation this way: "There can be no doubt that the threat of a labour tie-up along the Vancouver waterfront and at other British Columbia ports is having the effect of diverting grain to eastern ports for overseas shipment.
Nobody wants to store grain here that they may not be able to sell or remove.

As I have said, I want to thank the Minister of Transport for the cooperation he showed me. Can I ask the minister if he is now in a position to give an answer to the question I raised as to whether or not the national harbours board designs its structures according to local building bylaws? I heard unofficially that the minister took the matter very seriously and sent someone to Vancouver to investigate and explain the situation to the authorities in Vancouver. Could the minister give an answer?

I shall be glad to, Mr. Chairman. The answer is that the national harbours board designs the structures for the various harbours according to the latest national codes and standards and, in most cases, local building bylaws conform to these codes. In a few cases the local building bylaws might not agree with the national standards and, in such cases, if the local authorities present objections these are thoroughly investigated and if they appear reasonable steps are taken to conform to the local bylaws.
The designs used by the national harbours board are more or less standard and have been developed by the board's engineers from many years of experience on harbour works from coast to coast. On all important works there is a qualified resident engineer and inspection of materials is usually carried out by private inspection companies.
It is the board's practice to have all services installed to the satisfaction of the local authorities and as an example of this the following clauses were contained in the specification covering the construction of transit shed No. 2, centennial pier, Vancouver harbour:
Workmanship (re plumbing). The workmanship and method of installation shall conform to the best standard practice, to the entire approval of the engineer and shall be in accordance with local plumbing bylaws.
Inspection and Testing. All work included in the sprinkler system layout throughout the transit shed will be inspected and tested by and shall meet with the approval of the British Columbia underwriters association in all respects.
I trust that answers the hon. gentleman's query.

If there is anything that he wants information about that we have not in the books at this table I shall be glad to give it to him tomorrow.

I appreciate the minister's offer. I have not had any difficulty in the past in obtaining such information from the department or from the minister about specific items. I was thinking about a further explanation and clarification of some of these things for the general public and for other hon. members who may obtain these estimates, so that they could use the information to better advantage. The minister might take this under consideration and if he could give us some more detail it would be advantageous to everybody.
I should be very glad to look into it.
Before this item passes may I make an appeal to the minister to have a look at the rock outside Wesleyville harbour and see if a light could not be put on it.
Yes, I shall be glad to, Mr. Chairman.

Item agreed to.
412. Nautical services including Canada's share of the cost of the North Atlantic ice patrol: grants and contributions as detailed in the estimates: rewards for saving life from vessels in distress; subsidy to a salvage company; and the payment of expenses, including excepted expenses, incurred in respect of Canadian distressed seamen as defined in section 306 of the Canada Shipping Act, $604,524.

I do not wish to hold up the estimates but this is the only item that I can think of on which I can ask the minister what is the policy of the government as regards a coastguard service in British Columbia. This is, I think, one of the most intriguing and important points on our entire coast. It means very much to the fishermen and the entire services on that coast. Can the minister give us a complete picture of its status?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. We have appointed two co-ordinators, one on the west coast and one on the east coast, and we are in the process of appointing a co-ordinator for the central region of Canada. The co-ordinator has been appointed on the west coast and has taken office. He is now in the process of interviewing various groups on the west coast, the purpose of which is to find out how all of the marine services in that area at the present time can be best co-ordinated and used in the same way as the coastguard is used in the United States. We believe that with the equipment that is available, the ships and planes that are available, the main thing is now to have training and co-ordination. The working of all those groups in operation will, we feel sure, produce the equivalent of the United States coastguard.
I quite agree with the hon. member and with other hon. members who have brought this matter up in the house and have talked
Supply-Transport
with me personally that there is tremendous need for such a co-ordinated service in our waters, whether they be coastal or inland.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I say one word in connection with this and a brief one at that. I have read the press release issued by the Minister of Transport in connection with the coastguard service and the appointment of Captain Brand as director of marine operations. I think that was an excellent appointment but the minister will not mind my saying that I do not think a great deal has been added to the co-ordination as it existed prior to his press release. I say that because the significant point in the release is that there seems to have been no co-ordination in the Canadian coastal marine services of any vessels other than those operated by the Department of Transport. In other words, no new elements have been added. All that seems to have happened is a change in the name. It is a step in the right direction, of course, to co-ordinate the establishments of the Department of Transport; but if there is to be a proper rescue service and coastguard operation from one end of the country to the other, particularly on both coasts, this should be co-ordinated with the Canadian coastal marine services.
The minister will probably recall that the hon. member for Oxford was very keen about this from time to time and repeatedly complained that there was no suitable service on the great lakes. From the press release it did appear to me that there was really not much of a change in the search and rescue operations on both coasts. However, I may be mistaken here. I bring it to the attention of the minister because I think proper coordination should take place not only within the department but also outside of it.

I know the minister realizes how important this is to us on the west coast. He said that a co-ordinator had been appointed on each coast. He also said he thinks there will be on the coast of British Columbia a service similar to and as good as the coastguard service of the United States. What is the authority of the co-ordinator? If you are to have a coastguard service on the coast you must gave co-ordination and the co-operation of fishing boats, of the navy, of the R.C.A.F., of all weather, radio and other stations. What is the authority of the coordinator to bring them all together? Who has the say?

Under our direction the co-ordinator will have the authority to co-ordinate those various groups in search and rescue efforts. His job at the present time is to make a survey of the situation and report

Supply-Transport
to us what he considers is needed and then we will proceed to work on plans for training and co-ordinating the various vessels, government vessels and private vessels, so that they can be used in search and rescue work, which is the main objective of this exercise.

I have one small question I would like to ask the minister. It relates to the information in the details on page 523 under "nautical services". On this page are listed grants and contributions to mariners' or seamen's institutions, such as the navy league of Canada, Sydney, Nova Scotia, the seamen's mission society, Saint John, New Brunswick, and so on. Can the minister indicate what is the basis for these grants and what these particular missions, sailors' clubs or institutions do in so far as their assistance, if that is the proper name to give it, to seamen is concerned?
Then, there is an item "British Columbia towboat owners' association", toward which a grant is not required this year. The sum of $15,000 was granted to this association last year. Can the minister indicate what the $15,000 was for, and also what is the $75,000 item which is called a salvage subsidy to Foundation Maritime Limited, Montreal, Quebec? These amounts all come under the same item.

I am advised that the grants to institutions are for welfare work with sailors and maintaining hostels and things in ports where these sailors can go to. The $15,000 is to pay an adviser, one of the representatives of the tugboat owners, who co-ordinated certain rescue operations last year; and the $75,000 is to maintain a stand-by salvage tug in the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Atlantic waters area.

Just one other point. I understood the minister to say with respect to the $15,000 to the British Columbia towboat owners' association that this was a payment to a member or someone within that association who co-ordinated with or did some co-ordination work on search and rescue operations. Did he do somewhat similar work as will now be performed by the person the hon. minister referred to a while ago who will be appointed as co-ordinator?
In a much more limited field; only in regard to his own association.

Could the minister indicate what the results of this co-ordination were? Was the $15,000 well spent; did we get value for our money; and did anything concrete come out of it so far as sea rescue is concerned?
I am advised that the work done by the person was quite helpful but we considered it was not enough. That is why we have gone in for our own co-ordinator and embarked on this new plan.
I understand that money is paid for a standby tug for sea rescue work on the Atlantic coast, but there is no stand-by tug on the Pacific coast; is that correct?
It is a salvage tug on the Atlantic coast.
But not on the Pacific coast?

We did pay a similar subsidy for a salvage tug on the west coast, but I am advised that this was discontinued because there are a large number of salvage tugs on the west coast who perform this same function.

speechtext:
What I was going to ask the
minister was this, and it was apropos of the interruption I received from the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister when he referred to his speech in connection with the development of the Ottawa waterway. I think that is a very commendable project, but at the time it was not known what the depth of the locks over the sills would be. I put a question on the order paper, which I have here some place, and the answer given was that the depth over the sills would be nine feet. This means that the navigation depth is nine feet.
I do not see how the project of the hon. member, laudable as it might be and which I would be quite willing to support to the fullest extent, would be practical if ships of nine-foot draft only could be moved up and down the Ottawa river.
The nine-foot sill is correct, but the lock is constructed so that it can be deepened.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to say a word or two in relation to this matter. I agree with the minister that the bridge at Ste. Anne's is the key to the whole situation. I would hope that resulting from the discussions, which will have to take place between the government of Canada and the government of Quebec in connection with a new bridge which will leave the west end of the island of Montreal, there would be assurance that the bridge would be a high level bridge to make it possible for the Ottawa deep waterway to be constructed. I think it would be most unfortunate if we were to permit a new low level bridge to be built at the west end of the island of Montreal which would in any way prevent the future development of the waterway.
My understanding of what has taken place at Carillon in respect to the present construction is that while there are presently nine-foot sills to be put in, none the less the plans do call for the eventual deepening of these to 14 feet, and that there is no problem in relation to that being done under the existing plans, and that in the present power development there is by no means foreclosure of the eventual, and I hope fairly soon, achievement of the Ottawa deep waterway.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to add one comment. I am glad the hon. member for Carleton did make the interjection which he has. I have seen the plans on two occasions, and they are extremely interesting and intricate. Following the viewing of these plans and discussions of them with certain engineers I put a question on the order paper for the Minister of Public Works which, unfortunately, I have not got with me now.

Supply-Transport
However, the plans as they now stand provide for nine-foot navigation. It may be that in the future it will be possible to deepen the sills to 14 feet, but at increased cost because if there is to be 14-foot navigation the plans should be drawn now for that purpose. The plans are complete for the elevation of the bridges from the Ottawa-Hull area right down to the outflow of the Ottawa river into the St. Lawrence at Cascades. There can be no doubt from what I have seen that unless these plans are altered they provide at the moment for nine-foot navigation. Let me tell my hon. friend that in his anxiety to see the Ottawa waterway developed he will find support for it from this side of the house because I think it will be all to the good if there is an additional 14-foot waterway which flows into the St. Lawrence. But if that is to be done the plans will have to be altered.
Before the item carries I should like to assure the hon. member for Carleton that I agree with him in principle. If a new bridge is to be built, it should be a high level bridge.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not rising at this time to complain about the railway cars. This would be the last thing in the world which I would do, notwithstanding the fact that the minister's colleague, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, used to complain repeatedly about these amounts and once voted to remove one of these cars. Be that as it may, I am perfectly happy with this arrangement and I think it should remain as it is.
I rise to inquire about the Pelee island ferry service which comes under the steamship services. I asked this question on the supplementary estimates at the beginning of a session and the Minister of Finance, when he was dealing with the supplementaries, replied as follows, as reported at page 2114 of Hansard for 1959:
This is the way the operation was carried on previously. The ship had been operated before under just such an arrangement in the hon. gentleman's time when he was minister of transport.
I have since learned that statement is entirely inaccurate. The ship that is now being operated in the Pelee island service is not being operated by way of subsidy. This is a new ship and a departure has been made from the ordinary contract and policy of the department whereby instead of paying a steamship subvention a new ship is being
[Mr. Chevrier.3
purchased and turned over under certain terms and conditions to the company. Furthermore there has been a curtailment of the service. Whereas, in the first place, the S.S. Pelee operated not only between the mainland and Pelee island but also made daily calls at Sandusky, Ohio, in the United States, the United States portion of the trip has been cancelled. This was, I understand, the profitable part, the operation into the United States, and the other part was unprofitable.
I should like to say at once that nothing I have said is to be construed as criticism of the charming sponsor of the ship who I note, according to a press release, was the spouse of the hon. member for Essex South.

Mr. Chairman, I am advised, and I remember it well now because I think it was the first item I dealt with in the department when I took over in 1957, that the decision to build this ship was taken by the previous administration. It was to replace a ship that had worn out which, I believe, had been built in 1912 and had been classed as unsafe. It had been decided by the previous administration to build a new ship and that decision was carried out by this administration. The ship was for island-mainland service only and not for the United States and that decision, I am advised, was taken by the former administration and was carried out by this administration.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Was the decision made
earlier for the new ship as well?
Yes, it was made in 1956.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not contesting the minister's statement, but I should like to look into it. Perhaps I will have more to say when we come to the item of the maritime commission.
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

I just followed what the hon. member for Laurier had to say about these official railway cars. Undoubtedly an explanation has been given a number of times in the past, perhaps by the present minister, as to what these official railway cars are for and who uses them.

Two of these cars are used by the Governor General and three are for general use by the government, including ministers and the board of transport commissioners. The number in use has been decreased by two from the number previously in use when this government took office. At the present time I am considering making a study to see if one more of these cars can be eliminated.

It seems to me that perhaps there should be a reduction in the number

of railway cars. From what I can gather they are not used very often and consequently sit there perhaps as museum pieces more than anything else. With the advent of air transportation and it being increasingly more available to society and also to the cabinet perhaps in the near future we might not have such an item listed in the estimates.

The Governor General uses his two cars a great deal. The board of transport commissioners use one of the three remaining cars a great deal. As I say, I am now studying the possibility of eliminating another of the cars at present in use. As I mentioned earlier, we have reduced by two the number of cars that were previously in use.
I now have the answer to the question asked a few moments ago by the hon. member for Skeena. The answer is this. All ships of the Northland Navigation Company have been certified for service on the west coast as requested by the owner, with the exception of one passenger conveying vessel which was restricted to the number of passengers permitted on the certificate because its subdivision-that is the number of transfer bulkheads fitted-is below regulation standards.
That is for service on the west coast?
Yes; coastal waters.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not want to argue with the minister but my recollection is that when I held the position which the minister now holds there were five private cars and no more, namely two used by His Excellency the Governor General which were in constant use; one to the board of transport commissioners; one which was assigned to the minister of transport and one which was assigned to all the other ministers. That is the recollection I have. I may be in error.
I am glad the hon. member for Laurier has corrected me. We have eliminated not two cars but one car and at present are studying the elimination of another.

I wonder whether the minister could explain the reason for these amounts being listed here under the federal department. Is it because they relate in some cases to interprovincial travel? Why are the provincial governments-or in this instance Prince Edward Island particularly-not involved in building terminals or car ferries?
I ask this question as a result of comparing the situation with that in British Columbia where we also have ferry systems in operation between the mainland and Vancouver island and in some cases between points on the mainland. In so far as I know, all of them are operated under provincial government auspices. I wonder what the reason is for the difference there. Can the minister explain that matter to me?

Yes. These subsidies result from either the terms of union or confederation agreements between ourselves and these different provinces. They are of long standing,
5S22

Supply-Transport
with the exception of the agreement with Newfoundland which of course extends back only about 10 years. These services are operated on our behalf by Canadian National Railways.

Are all these votes in accordance with the terms of confederation? Are they all interprovincial services or are not some of them just within the province itself? I notice one or two here that are within a particular province. It is not often that I agree with the hon. member for Skeena but one thing that puzzles me is why the Department of Transport will provide certain services in the maritimes or the eastern provinces and will not provide them in the west.
These ferries are all the result of confederation terms with the exception of the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry.
There is one with respect to Pelee island. Is that one of the terms of confederation?
Will the hon. member tell me what item he was talking about? I thought he was referring to the Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland ferry service.

I was speaking generally of these items, but I saw it some place. As a matter of fact, every time I look through these items I get a little bit annoyed; it is not that I am not in favour of their having these services down in the maritimes and in the east, but as a matter of comparison, the situation annoys me. I saw an item some place with regard to a ferry to Pelee island. Is that an interprovincial ferry?
This new Pelee island ferry was an arrangement entered into in 1956 by the previous administration and carried on by this government.
